*Do penance.* The same things which the herald preaches: [0087B] that it may be shown that he is no other than he who had cried in the voice. For Christ is the Word which cries in the Jordan by his instrument, and in all who from the beginning spoke anything by divine inspiration: and yet this man alone is the voice, because through him is shown the Word present, which the others announced from afar. For between the voice and the word there is nothing between, but as soon as the voice has sounded, straightway the word is perceived: as John, shut up, ceased: Christ shone forth in mighty works. Whence John is the figure of the prophets and of the law, who are truly the voice of the crying wisdom of God, of whom John is the end, and when they cease the Word alone, which had sounded in them, is shown by itself.

[n: (RAB.)] This preaching of Christ, begun in Capharnaum with miracles flashing forth, is said, etc., *as far as* he began to preach when the Baptist was imprisoned.

[0087C]VERS. 18.-- *Who is called Peter.* Either when Andrew first brought him to him, this name was put upon him, when it is said: *Thou shalt be called Cephas [n: (Joan. I)]*, which is interpreted *Peter:* although here he seems to promise it for the future. Or when he confessed: *Thou art Christ the Son of the living God,* it was said to him: *Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church [n: (Matth. XVI)]*.

[n: (BEDA.)] Peter, *acknowledging:* Andrew, *manly:* which befits teachers: because these alone, etc., *as far as* but because the first man went out disobedient, the second entered in obedient [n: (RAB.)] Matthew says that he called the disciples after his dwelling at Capharnaum. John says, etc., *as far as* but before Jesus came into Cana of Galilee, Andrew brought Peter, yet [0087D] they were not disciples.



## CHAPTER IV. (cont.)

*Casting a net.* Because those whom he sees often gaping after earthly gains he calls to heavenly desires, and through them, by the nets of the Gospel, he snatches others out of the deep of iniquity, whence he adds: *Come ye after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men [n: (Joan. I)]*.

VERS. 19.-- *Fishers.* He who is about to fish goes through the places of fishing.

Mystically. When being incarnate he took flesh, he saw by his divinity in the sea of the world spiritual fishers: and to others he showed what they were, whom he had foreseen from eternity.

VERS. 20.-- *Immediately.* Perfect obedience is to leave one's own things unfinished. Their nets being left: because even [0088A] if afterwards they take them up again, it is not out of covetousness and the love of ownership. In these a pattern is given to those who wish to follow. The intention is changed, not the fishing, the nets are changed into doctrine, covetousness into the love of souls: the sea becomes the world, the ship the Church, the fishes good and evil men.

VERS. 21.-- *He saw two others.* Behold, in these four the number of the evangelists is prefigured, who draw souls out of the world from the four quarters of the world.

They are called two and two, because charity is not save between two. A calling is spoken of: either according to the election of grace. Whence it is said: *Whom he called [n: (Rom. VIII)]*, etc. Or according to that word: *Many are called [n: (Matth. X)]*.

[n: (AUG.)] It is asked how Matthew and Mark say that Jesus called them two by two: first Peter and Andrew, etc., *as far as* but he sent unlettered fishermen [0088B] to preach for this reason, that faith might be reckoned to stand in the power of God, not in the eloquence of men.

*Of Zebedee, and John.* Zebedee, a fugitive, that is, the devil. James, a supplanter, who is helped by John, that is, by the grace of God. *And he called them. But they,* etc. He called others also, but it suffices to name these.

VERS. 23.-- *And Jesus went about all Galilee.* His fellow workers being called, he presses on with preaching, teaching that a teacher ought to be untiring. *Teaching in the synagogues.* Teaching about morals, those subject to the active life. Preaching about things to come, those perfect in the contemplative life. Teaching the natural righteousnesses, namely chastity and humility and the like, which man has by nature. Preaching the Gospel of the kingdom. To the Gospel belongs [0088C] the mystery of righteousness, a good beginning, the promise of beatitude, the remission of sins, adoption, resurrection, the heavenly inheritance, the fellowship of the angels.

*In the synagogues.* Nor let an idle teacher run about to no purpose, but let him preach where there are many.

*The Gospel.* Because righteousness is a trouble to one living in the flesh, the labor of righteousness is not undertaken unless the wage of the work be looked for. Therefore Christ preaches beatitude for good news, that he may stir men up to patience in good work.

*And healing.* To cure sickness and infirmity was no great thing, since they were to die afterwards. But it was done for this reason, that they might so be raised up to the kingdom. Morally instructing preachers to minister earthly supports also to their subjects, and so to draw them to the kingdom.

VERS. 24.-- *And his fame went abroad. [n: (BEDA.)]* The works of salvation [0088D] do not shine out enough to hearers without the fame of a good odor, nor does fame profit without the work: without which, etc., *as far as* he cures bodies, that they may the more readily hear invisible things. Otherwise it was a small thing to spend care upon men soon to die.

VERS. 25.-- *They followed. [n: (AUG.)]* Fourfold crowds, namely. Some, etc., *as far as* others, wishing out of envy to accuse him and to catch him in something.



## CHAPTER V.

VERS. 1.-- *And Jesus seeing. [n: (AUG.)]* With this Luke agrees, saying: *And it came to pass in those days, he went out into a mountain to pray [n: (Luc. VI)]*, etc. But Luke says, etc., *as far as* for not all men can do all things: [0089A] which is thought the truer, although the same [sermon] of both may be seen to have been delivered at once.

*He went up.* Teaching his own to go up and not to remain in the crowd: being about to teach a higher righteousness than that which is of the Scribes and the Pharisees. He himself, a mountain, went up into a mountain, that he might teach the higher summits of the virtues, and might show that the Church, above which he sits preaching, is to be raised more loftily by the Lord's precept, which the same teaching would more fully instruct unto the end of the world. He leads the apostles apart more eminently, that from the mountain the mountains may first receive peace for the people. *He was set down.* The sitting is of the humanity, by which he is known. Whence: *And the world knew him not,* before the incarnation. *They came.* That they may hear the nearer, who hasten in mind to fulfil.

[0089B]VERS. 2.-- *And opening.* The opening of the mouth signifies the depth of the sacrament. He opened as it were an abyss, as it were a treasure, as it were a river of paradise. On this mountain he writes the New Testament in the hearts of sons, beginning from beatitude, who on mount Sinai gave the Old Testament on stones to servants, beginning from terror.

[n: (AUG.)] The sermon which our Lord spoke on the mountain, as in the Gospel, etc., *as far as, Everyone who hears these my words and shall do them, I will liken him to a wise man [n: (Matth. VII)]*. [var: Vulg. Mt 7:24 *Omnis ergo qui audit verba mea haec, et facit ea, assimilabitur viro sapienti*]

VERS. 3.-- *Blessed. [n: (GREG. NYSS.)]* Beatitude, as my opinion carries it, is the comprehension of all those things which, etc., *as far as* for misery is a wretchedness in bitter and sorrowful chances [0089C] and calamities that do not fall out by our own will.

*Blessed are the poor.* The number of the sentences is to be diligently attended to. For beatitude begins from humility.

*[n: (HIER.)] Blessed are the poor in spirit.* Because it is not necessity but faith, and the devotion of poverty, that makes men blessed, etc., *as far as* as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, so poverty is the beginning of beatitude.

[n: (CHRYSOST.)] The poor in spirit are the humble and contrite of heart. And by spirit he here means the soul and the will. But because many are humble not of their own accord, but constrained by necessity, he calls the first sort blessed.

VERS. 4.-- *Blessed are the meek.* The meek are those who master evil habits: perfect virtue is the possession of one's habits.

[0089D] [n: (THEOPH.)] The meek are not those who are not angry at all, etc., *as far as* so the doctrine of a man is discerned through patience.

*They shall possess the land. [n: (AUG.)]* That land I believe to be the one of which it is said in the Psalm: *Thou art my hope, my portion in the land of the living [n: (Psal. CLXI)]*.

VERS. 5.-- *Blessed are they that mourn.* For their own sins or for others', which mourning is from the lower watering, but that which comes from the upper watering is out of desire for the heavenly country. The one washes present filth, the other kindles more sharply the lovers of eternal things. But he who has laid down his sins, has corrected his habits by meekness, and has wept besides, can now hunger and thirst after righteousness, which before he could not. This [0090A] virtue is not fulfilled without the spirit of fortitude: because through him, by hungering, we shall one day come to fulness. *Blessed are they that mourn.* It remains, after the things aforesaid, to purge by mourning the foulness of our ruins. Mourning for sins or out of heavenly desire earns consolation, and no other does.

These are enlightened by the spirit of knowledge, that they may know in what evils they are wrapped.

[n: (HILAR.)] For those that mourn, not for those grieving over bereavements, or insults, or losses, but for those weeping over their old sins, and made wretched by the consciousness of the crimes with which we are befouled, this assiduous consolation is prepared in heaven.

VERS. 6.-- *Blessed are they that hunger.* Lovers of the good word, to whom it is not enough that they are just, but they always thirst for the work of righteousness.

[0090B]Righteousness is to render to each his own, to oneself, and to one's neighbors, and to God. This righteousness will not be fully fulfilled until God be all in all: therefore here we can hunger, not be filled. The light of righteousness is mercy, the strength of mercy is righteousness; this mercy has need of the spirit of counsel, without which no one is merciful with circumspection. The beginning is to have mercy on oneself, the end is to die for another. For the order of showing mercy is that each man begin from himself. Christ hints at the end, having died out of mercy for sinners.

VERS. 7.-- *Blessed are the merciful.* Mercy is born of the things that go before, because if true humility has gone before, and the mind grows meek, and weeps for its own falls and others', and hungers after righteousness, afterwards true mercy is born. For then it will make others' miseries its own [0090C] and will help according to its powers: and if the means of helping is wanting, compassion will not be wanting: *Be ye merciful as your Father also is merciful [n: (Luc. VI)]*, that is, let us have mercy unto that end unto which God also has mercy, that goodness may overflow upon all: mercy without righteousness is called remission and lukewarmness; righteousness without mercy is called severity and harshness.

VERS. 9.-- *Blessed are the peacemakers. [n: (RAB.)]* The peacemakers are those who compose all the motions of the mind and subject them to reason, because nothing resists those who are like the Father, etc., *as far as* but when God shall be all in all, then the beatitude of adoption will be given.

VERS. 10.-- *Blessed are they that suffer persecution.* In the seven aforesaid there is the showing and the proving of perfection. Those who have the aforesaid things can suffer persecution: and [0090D] he rightly holds the aforesaid things which he has received who is ready to die for them.

VERS. 11.-- *Blessed are you when they shall revile you.* Thus far he set down his sentences generally, as though to those absent, although they belonged to those present also, now he turns his words to them (although this belongs to others also), foretelling how great things they should suffer for his name: because he wished to make known to them the dignity of their rank, saying: *You are the salt of the earth, you are the light of the world;* that from the sad things they might take humility, from the glad things consolation.

*Shall revile.* The ancient translation has: *When men shall hate you, and shall say all that is evil, and shall cast you out.* Yet the sense is the same in ours, since revilings come from hatred of the heart. He who chooses the glory of heaven does not [0091A] fear reproach on earth; as much as each man rejoices at the praise of men, so much does he grieve at reproach. Him whom praise lifts up, blame casts down: where a man seeks to be praised only before God, he does not fear to be confounded in the sight of men. *Lying.* He adds this, lest he glory of whom evil things are truly said. He adds also: *For my sake,* because sometimes false things are said, which comes about through the rashness of men, yet they do not suffer this for Christ's sake, whom they do not follow.

VERS. 12.-- *For your reward is very great in heaven.* Not in rolling things, since an eternal reward ought not to be in rolling things, but in spiritual firmaments, where everlasting righteousness dwells. Already therefore they feel this reward who rejoice in spiritual goods. But it will be made perfect when this mortal shall put on [0091B] immortality. *For so they persecuted,* etc. He tempers the rigor of the passion by an example. Persecution is made in three ways: by hatred of the heart, by words, by deeds.

VERS. 13.-- *You are the salt of the earth.* Here now is shown the office of the apostles, namely that they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world. This belongs especially to the apostles, who ought to be adorned with the aforesaid virtues, namely poverty and the rest, that they may be the best salt, seasoning others by doctrine and by the example of their own life. Salt, health from corruption. Whence the prophet: *I have set thee for a light of the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the ends of the earth.* [var: Vulg. Is 49:6 *dedi te in lucem gentium, ut sis salus mea usque ad extremum terrae*; Act 13:47 has *Posui te in lucem gentium, ut sis in salutem*]

*But if the salt,* etc. That is, if you, by whom others are to be seasoned, give way before adverse or prosperous things: by whom shall error be taken away from you, when God has chosen [0091C] to raise you up for others? It is good for nothing: because (as another evangelist says) it is useful neither to the earth, which by being cast upon it it hinders from sprouting, nor to the dunghill, which it does not suffer to grow fruitful. So he who goes backward neither bears fruit himself, nor is able to till others, but is cast out of the Church, and is laughed at in these words: *This man began to build, and was not able to finish. If the salt shall lose its savor [n: (Luc. IV)]*. That is, if through fear or through greed the teacher has let go the savor of wisdom, by whom shall his foolishness be amended? This befits the apostles alone: what follows befits all masters: *It is good for nothing any more,* etc. At the end he concludes thus concerning all: *Unless your righteousness abound,* etc.

*And be trodden upon by men.* The holy and true minister of Christ, even if he is laughed at by the wicked, cannot [0091D] be trodden upon, because fixed in mind he remains in heaven.

VERS. 14.-- *You are the light of the world.* Salt before light, because life before doctrine: life leads to the knowledge of truth. He who fears God does not lack knowledge.

*The light of the world.* There is another cause why they ought not to fail: because they are enlightened by Christ in word and in example: wherever they are carried among worldly men they ought to minister the light of faith and of knowledge. And as (because they are salt) they ought to drive away corruption: so also they ought to put darkness (because they are light) to flight.

*A city cannot,* etc. Because the apostles are foundations, they are fitly called a city. *Upon a mountain.* The place hints at the mountain of righteousness, which is lofty, whereby you are made public [0092A] so that you may not hide yourselves. For there is no power of slipping away or of doing anything in secret; therefore rule your subjects mercifully within by counsel, and without against adversaries defend them by fighting for righteousness: which belongs to the spirit of counsel and of fortitude.

VERS. 15.-- *Neither do they light a lamp.* By household examples he teaches them not to hide the light of the word committed to them. They do not light, that is, the doctrine of preaching was not given for this, that they should hide it and subject it to the servitude of the body, while they fear certain things. But let them subject their body to the ministry of God, that through the voice and the other offices of the body the light may appear more excellent than the rest. Whence it is said [n: (I Cor. IX)]: *I chastise my body,* etc. Or, Christ lit a lamp, when he filled the earthen shell of human nature with the flame of his divinity: [0092B] which he neither hid from believers, nor shut up under a bushel, that is, the measure of the law, or within the bounds of a single nation. But upon the candlestick, that is, the Church, he fastened the faith of his incarnation, where all can behold it who are in the house, that is, in the Church, or in the world. Whence he adds: *So let your light shine,* etc. *A candlestick.* As Christ is the lamp, the candlestick is the cross, upon which he was to be lifted up. The candlestick is the Church, which bears the word of the present life.

VERS. 16.-- *So let your light shine,* etc. And do all these things in such a way that you do not set the end of your good work in the praises of men. *That they may see,* etc. I require works, that they may be seen, and that so the doctrine may be confirmed: and this not to your own glory.

VERS. 17.-- *Do not think.* After he had exhorted them [0092C] to suffer all things for the truth, and not to hide it, and to work the glory of God, he begins to teach what they are to teach. As if he were saying: What is this that thou forbiddest to be hidden, for which thou biddest all things to be suffered? is there anything against the law? *I am not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil,* [var: Vulg. Mt 5:17 *non veni solvere, sed adimplere*, without *legem* in the second clause] either by doing what it says, or by supplying what was lacking and imperfect.

VERS. 18.-- *One jot. [n: (BEDA.)]* Here it is shown that the things which are thought least in the law are full of spiritual sacraments, and all things, etc., *as far as* because the jot signifies ten, that is, the decalogue, whose apex is the perfection of the Gospel.

*All things be fulfilled.* Let them be spiritually fulfilled, or let the imperfect be perfected, and let the things that signify be consummated, that is, by the fulfilment.



## CHAPTER V. (cont.)

[0092D]VERS. 19.-- *He therefore that shall break,* etc. The least things are the cross of Christ and his passion, and he who is ashamed of them is least; he who confesses them is great. Or he marks the Pharisees, who let go the commandments of God for their own traditions, which are worth nothing, while they pass over even the least thing that is in the law. But morally he breaks it who does not fulfil it, but holds it as these things were given to the weak. Or he who does not understand it spiritually. To break, is not to do what one rightly understands, or not to understand what one does not distort, or to lessen the wholeness of Christ's superadding.

*He shall be called the least,* etc. In the kingdom of heaven he shall be called least who will be unworthy in it, in which there is none least but all are great.

[0093A] *But he that shall do.* He who shall not break it, and so teaches, is not least, yet not great: but he does what he teaches. *For only the doers of the law are just before God [n: (Rom. II)]*. [var: Vulg. Rom 2:13 *Non enim auditores legis justi sunt apud Deum, sed factores legis justificabuntur*]

VERS. 20.-- *But I say to you.* [var: Vulg. Mt 5:20 *Dico enim vobis*] When he says, I say, he struck in a great force and a deep understanding for thinking: he shows how he superadds. And he does not undo the things he had commanded before. It is even more to love enemies than not to hate them: not to covet, than not to commit adultery: not to be angry, than not to kill.

*Unless,* etc. That is, you shall fulfil not only the least precepts of the law, but also those which I add: because while the things added are done unto perfection, these too are more fully performed which were set down before unto a beginning: [0093B] because he who does not look upon a woman to lust after her, neither does he commit fornication: nor does he kill who is not angry.

*Your righteousness.* He calls the righteousness of the Pharisees all those things actually commanded for the worship of God: or the mystical things of the figures, established only according to the letter.

VERS. 21.-- *You have heard,* etc. He sets forth what the righteousness of the Pharisees is, and he who fulfils it is not at once great, but has climbed some step.

VERS. 22.-- *But I,* etc. He begins to unfold the perfection which he came to fulfil, and how their righteousness ought to abound the more.

*Everyone who is angry.* Because they did not know that anything was murder except a killing: he discloses that every motion of the mind toward doing harm is reckoned as murder. The commandment of Christ is not contrary to the law, but more broadly [0093C] contains the law in itself. He who is not angry does not kill. But not conversely, the leave to be angry is the cause of murder. Take away anger, and murder is not committed.

VERS. 23.-- *If therefore thou offer thy gift.* He unfolds the fuller righteousness by showing that if it is not lawful to be angry with a brother, much less is it lawful to keep in the mind that which seeks to be turned into hatred. If we have anything of evil in the mind against a neighbor, we cannot offer to God in a way that pleases him. *If therefore thou offer.* According to the letter this is absurd. There is therefore in the inner temple an altar, that is, faith, upon which any gift whatsoever, that is, a psalm, a hymn, a prayer, and the like, unless it rest, will not be pleasing to God. *And there,* etc., that is, when in the heart (which is the inner temple) thou art about to offer such a gift, if it should come into thy mind [0093D] that thy brother has something against thee, whom thou hast wronged. For if he has wronged thee, it is not he, but thou who hast something against him: nor is it needful for thee then to seek pardon, but to give it, as thou wishest to be forgiven thyself.

VERS. 24.-- *Leave there,* etc. He does not say, Carry it back: because what is rightly offered may not be changed. But leave it, until thou mayest offer it more acceptably: for he does not drive back the gift, but seeks charity toward one's neighbor, without which no one comes to the charity of God. Whence: Let him first pay charity to his neighbor who desires his gift to please God. *Go.* Not with the feet, but in mind mayest thou humbly prostrate thyself before him in the sight of him to whom thou art about to offer. Or by seeking pardon if he is present. *Thou shalt offer.* This is from the spirit of piety, whereby a man becomes meek, and understands the divine word [0094A] piously, and by understanding obeys, and lifts up his heart to fulfil it.

VERS. 25.-- *Be at agreement.* As he has already commanded a man to be reconciled to his brother, and afterwards bids that enemies be loved, so here, while we run in the way of this world, he exhorts to peace and concord, as it is said: *If it be possible, as much as is in you, having peace with all men [n: (Rom. XII)]*. And in place of "consenting" the Greek has "kindly" or "well-disposed." *Quickly,* lest thou put it off till the morrow: *While thou art in the way,* while it is still lawful to work.

If thou hast wronged a brother, be reconciled to him. If an adversary has arisen, be well-disposed, that he may become a friend.

*In the way with him.* The divine word is with us in the way of Christ. The adversary is with us in the way of the world. [0094B] The divine word is to us the way in which we run. Whence: *I have run the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*.

*Lest perhaps he deliver thee up.* He so tempered it, that it should not bring in a place of repentance: for it might be thought that if the adversary had died and one could not be well-disposed to him in the way, he would necessarily be delivered up to the judge. But he both left a place of repentance, and delivered the impenitent up to the judge, saying: Let the judge deliver thee to the officer. *Let him deliver thee up,* that is, let him be the cause why thou art delivered into the hands of Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgment. Christ to the officer, that is, to the angel, who shall gather the cockle.

VERS. 26.-- *The last farthing.* That is, small sins, because nothing will be unpunished. Or by the last farthing are signified earthly sins, [0094C] because the first part of the world is heaven; the second, air; the third water; the fourth, and last, earth. Therefore until thou repay the last farthing, that is, until thou pay for the sins which thou hast contracted from the earth.

VERS. 27.-- *You have heard. [n: (RAB.)]* Still he who said: *I am not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil [n: (Marc. XI)]*. He adds: how much it ought to abound, etc., *as far as* when the soul, having left the higher law, is corrupted, prostituted by a base will for lower things.

*Shall look upon a woman. [n: (BEDA.)]* A great superadding. Sight is put for every motion which is, etc., *as far as* because a man is accused or defended out of his conscience not according to what he was able to do and was not permitted, but according to what he willed and purposed.

*To lust after her.* That it may pass over into the affection of the heart, [0094D] so that he sets himself to do it, where the will is not wanting, but the occasion: which is called passion, which is death in the house. Pro-passion is a sudden affection of the mind, either of anger or of love. Passion is a form or deliberation of the mind out of consent. Whence a man is called wrathful or a lover.

[n: (ISID.)] If contemplation turns into weariness or into arrogance, let it go, and pass over to the active life: because it is better to be saved through the active than to perish through the contemplative.

VERS. 29.-- *Pluck it out.* According to the letter no member is commanded to be plucked out, but the inner sight, which is called the right, and the outer, which is called the left, if it hurts, is to be called back or removed by the zeal of dutiful labor: and [0095A] even to be put far away, so that it may not so much as be held in memory. The eye is plucked out when an evil habit is broken. It is cast away when it is wholly brought to nothing, nor is it suffered to enter.

VERS. 30.-- *Thy right hand.* Prosperous working, or some vigorous helper within the business of life: and if he is a scandal in the law of God, it is better to be saved with him cut off than to be damned along with him. *Cut it off,* etc. If anyone preaches this of the bodily members, he ought not to be listened to out of any affection of dutifulness. But that from thence the wickedness of habits and the crookedness of actions may be cut away, so that whatever in the eye of the mind overturns us from the way of righteousness and from uprightness of habits, and whatever beats without against the working of the virtues, may be driven far off. *Into hell.* The name of gehenna is not found among the ancients: but is first set down by the [0095B] Lord. The occasion of that name is this. The idol of Baal was beside Jerusalem at the foot of mount Moria, where Siloe was. This valley was well-watered and wooded and full of delights, and a place in it was consecrated to idols: but the people of Israel went so far in madness that, leaving the temple, they sacrificed there, and burned their own sons to demons. And that place was called Gehennon, that is, the valley of Ennon. And God threatens that he will fill that place with corpses, so that it may be called polyandrum, that is, a burial-mound of the dead: by the name of this place therefore the punishments to come are designated.

VERS. 31.-- *Let him give her. [n: (AUG.)]* [var: Vulg. Mt 5:31 *det ei libellum repudii*] Moses wrote in Deuteronomy that if a wife does not please her husband on account of some foulness, he should put her away. Which Christ expounds, etc., *as far as* as he loves an enemy, not in [0095C] this, that he is an enemy and evil, but that he is a man, so that he may be saved along with him.

[n: (CHRYSOST.)] Moses permitted a bill of divorce to be given, lest for hatred's sake blood should be shed. He permitted evils to be done, etc., *as far as* because we cannot forbid to the full the evil wills of men.

VERS. 32.-- *By reason of fornication.* Because in this the faith of chastity and of wedlock is broken: and he does not make her commit adultery, but she herself is the cause of her own guilt. But if he puts her away for fornication, he ought to be free from fornication himself, nor is it lawful to marry another while she lives. *By reason of fornication.* Of the woman, who has committed fornication, or of the man, lest he commit fornication, namely if the wife compels him to idolatry, or to avarice, or to other unlawful lusts. For fornication is not only of defilement, [0095D] but generally that which makes a man stray from the law of God. *And he that,* etc. [n: (CHRYSOST.)] Do not say that her husband has put her away, because even after she is put away, she remains the wife of him who put her away.

VERS. 33.-- *But thou shalt render.* If it should happen that thou swear: thou shalt swear by the Creator: not by a creature. For each man venerates that by which he swears: this he loves, this he fears. Therefore the law commands that no oath be sworn save by God.

*But I,* etc. He teaches that there is nothing so cheap among creatures that a man ought to forswear himself by it, since he forbids the oath from the highest to the lowest, that is, from heaven to a hair. He is convicted of forswearing himself against God, whose throne is heaven, and whose is whatever is.

[0096A] *By heaven.* They either supposed heaven to be something more, or, swearing by it, did not think themselves held by an oath: therefore he so tempers the sentence, that heaven may be believed to be a creature of God, and not something more: and that, because it is his throne, perjury may be feared. So also concerning the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet. He therefore who swears by a creature owes the oath to him who created and rules it, nor is it rightly thought to be paid to another.

Let us not swear by creatures so as to venerate them beyond what we ought by them, so as to esteem them cheap, namely so that when we swear by them we should think we swear by nothing.

*Nor by the earth.* Others swear by the safety of Pharao, who by the judgment of God is set among the lowest. *There is no power but from God [n: (Rom. XIII)]*: and in this thou swearest by God.

[0096B] *Nor,* etc. Because it is not thy work, but God's: and so in the least things, by swearing by God, thou canst incur perjury.

He who swears by his head owes it to him whose image and power abides in it.

VERS. 36.-- *For thou canst not,* etc. Since these things aforesaid are hard and difficult, no one keeps them without the spirit of fortitude. He drives men to perfection, while he takes away the occasion of swearing.

VERS. 37.-- *Yea, yea; no, no.* He says it twice for this reason, that what thou sayest with the mouth thou mayest prove by works. What thou deniest in words, thou mayest not approve or confirm by deeds.



## CHAPTER V. (cont.)

He did not altogether forbid swearing, but the occasion of perjury. He taught what is more perfect, showing that what goes beyond is of evil. The Apostle swears, that he may persuade [0096C] to faith: the Church too, for the sake of a covenant of peace and of faith, grants her own to swear. But Christ taught what is more perfect, indulged what belonged to weakness, cut away what was superstitious.

The truth of the Gospel does not admit an oath, but another's weakness compels it, so long as he does not believe the truth.

*It is of evil.* Not indeed evil, because although not good, yet necessary, but it is of evil, not of thine, but of his by whom thou art compelled to swear, that is, of that weakness of his which is an evil.

VERS. 38.-- *You have heard. [n: (AUG.)]* The law appointed a measure of vengeance: an eye for an eye. But if it can be said, etc., *as far as* but out of love of justice, the just for the unjust, which is good for evil, which the judge also does.

[0096D]As to what he says, *an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth:* he does not wish to take away the one, but to preserve both, while he threatens retaliation. Which he also does with measure, that the vengeance may not exceed the injury: and this is the beginning of peace, and as it were the commencement of justice.

VERS. 39.-- *Not to resist.* The justice of the law instructs the untaught in the beginning of justice, that is, to repay no more than was inflicted. The justice of the Gospel (which leads men to the kingdom) is not to resist evil: *Not to resist:* as he himself likewise: *Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart [n: (Matth. XI)]*. And David: *If I have repaid them that repaid me evils [n: (Psal. VII)]*. Jerem. *And I have given my cheek to him that struck me [n: (Thren. III)]* [var: Vulg. Lam 3:30 *Dabit percutienti se maxillam*, "He shall give his cheek to him that striketh him"]. Behold, the same Lord of the law and of the Gospel.

[0097A] *Offer to him.* Not only shouldst thou not strike back, but if he wishes to strike the other cheek, bear it patiently: this concerning injury to the body. But as to necessary things, if thou hast lost one, allow the remainder also to be taken away. What then of things superfluous?

*The other. [n: (CHRYSOST.)]* First, it is an unworthy thing that a faithful man [sic: *nomo*] should stand in judgment before the sight of an unbelieving judge. For even if he be an unbeliever, etc., *as far as* If once thou hast entered into judgment, thou dost no longer desire that the truth of the cause should appear, but that in whatever way thou mayest come off victor.

VERS. 40.-- *And to him who,* etc. It is counsel, before thou contend. It is indeed lawful for the weak to demand back their own, but not to contend. Luke conversely: He that taketh away thy garment, forbid not thy coat also. Which is to be done not concerning these things alone, but concerning all temporal things. *Thy [0097B] coat.* Or, the coat is the soul, which if a man be unwilling to lose, let him give up his cloak, that is, his body to martyrdom. Spiritually, the teacher takes away the coat when he makes a man confess his inward vices, such as envy, pride, and the like. He adds: *And the cloak;* he who does not blush to confess the outward ones also, such as theft and fornication.

VERS. 41.-- *A thousand paces.* This is a sabbath day's journey, by which spiritual perfection is signified: because it is not lawful to do servile work on the sabbath. *Other two.* He goes other two also who, while he is reduced to servitude in body only, is ready to be reduced in spirit and soul, that is, in reason and in will.

VERS. 42.-- *Give to him.* Such things as can be given honourably and justly. If the means be wanting, give the affection by a word or by a service. [0097C] *Give to him.* So, namely, that it hurt neither thee nor another: for justice is to be weighed. For thus wilt thou give to everyone that asketh, and if not that which he asks, yet something better, when thou shalt have corrected him that asks unjustly. *And to him that would borrow.* He embraces two kinds of bestowing. For either we give of good will, or we lend to one who will repay. And sometimes he who gives is unwilling to lend, as though there were no reward in it when the debtor pays back the thing received. But truly he who commands even this, repays. He says therefore: *Turn not away,* that is, nor alienate thy will. *For God loveth a cheerful giver [n: (II Cor. IX)]*, and so the spiritual teacher ought to put out to his hearers the interest of the divine word, that he may be able to receive from them the recompense of a good work, and to hope for a reward from God.

VERS. 43.-- *You have heard.* He who came to fulfil the law leads at the [0097D] end to full charity, which is the fulfilling of the law.

*Thou shalt hate.* Perhaps it is to be understood according to what is above: *An eye for an eye,* etc. Or by withdrawing the offices of humanity.

VERS. 44.-- *Love.* The Church is fought against in three ways: by hatred, by words, by the torment of the body. The Church on the contrary loves, does good, prays. This is the new commandment, this makes, out of sons of wrath, sons of God; whence there follows: *That you may be sons.* The adoption of sons is acquired by charity alone.

*Do good.* By ministering food to the mind or to the body. Which he also does who says that such a one is not even to take food. For all these things look to this, that they may become brethren. [0098A] Single things are set against single, that all the parts of malice may be overcome by goodness. The imprecations of the prophets seem to be against this, which are not uttered by the wish of those desiring, but by the spirit of those foreseeing.

*Pray. [n: (AUG.)]* He does not say this for brethren, in whom there are sometimes sins graver than the persecution of enemies, etc., *as far as* although they confess that they have sinned, and vehemently repent of having done evil, yet they have such dispositions of mind that they do not humble themselves to ask pardon.

But it may move one, that John in his Epistle seems to admonish, concerning the love of God and of the neighbour, only that we should love the brethren, whereas the Lord says that prayer is to be made even for enemies. But by brethren are understood not only those who already believe, but those who are to believe, for whom [0098B] prayer must be made, that they may be joined to us by a brotherly covenant.

VERS. 45.-- *Sons.* Not degenerate. As if he should say: Having received the power, act by works that you may be sons by being born again through charity. *Of the Father.* He is already called Father. See that you be sons born again of God, who is charity. *Who maketh his sun to rise.* This visible one. For they say in the book of Solomon, *The sun of justice hath not shined upon us [n: (Sap. V)]* [var: Vulg. Sap 5:6 *justitiae lumen non luxit nobis*, "the light of justice hath not shined upon us"]. And of the rain of doctrine the prophet says: *Upon one city it rained, and not upon another. His sun [n: (Amos. IV)]* [var: Vulg. Am 4:7 *et plui super unam civitatem, et super alteram civitatem non plui*, "and I rained upon one city, and upon another city I rained not"], etc. As if he should say: Whom he made, whose properly are all the things which he created out of nothing. What then shall we do concerning those things which we have received of his gift?

VERS. 46.-- *The publicans.* The exactors of the Romans, whom the Jews so call, because they bore the charge of the commonwealth. They are also said to have drawn their name from Publius, a Roman [0098C] king, who first appointed them.

VERS. 47.-- *And if you salute.* If you shall have prayed for those only who are joined to you by some kinship, what more has your benefit than that of unbelievers? Brethren must be loved, and humbly saluted: but it is little.

VERS. 48.-- *Perfect.* In the love of God and of the neighbour. The crown of perfection is to love even enemies, and to pray for them, as Christ also did.



## CHAPTER VI.

VERS. 1.-- *Take heed,* etc. He who hitherto has given precept concerning mercy, now gives precept concerning cleanness of heart, by which God is seen. For if not with a simple intention but for the praise of men, the works [0098D] of mercy are not approved by God. The praise of men ought not to be sought, but to follow, that by example it may invite others. Thus far concerning the justice of the Gospel, which is above the justice of the Scribes and Pharisees. Now with what cleanness of heart that same justice ought to be fulfilled: which is observed in almsgiving and in prayer. For he does not here admonish either to pray or to give alms: but with what mind we ought to do it. For the matter here is of cleansing the heart. *With your Father.* Whose glory sons ought to seek, and to refer all good things to this, that they may please him.

VERS. 2.-- *When therefore,* etc. From the whole to the parts, that he may set forth what good things are not to be done for the praise of men. *To sound a trumpet.* Perhaps they did this for the sake of calling men together: that all might go as if to a spectacle. [0099A] *Before thee.* He sounds a trumpet before himself who wishes to be praised before others: that he may appear greater than they. *They have received.* From God, the inspector of the heart, the punishment of their deceit, of whom it is said: *Depart from me, you crafty workers: for you have had my name: but you have not done my works.*

VERS. 3.-- *Let it not know.* The left hand, vices: the right hand, virtues. What therefore virtue does, let not elation know, nor vainglory, nor any vice: but let the light of right working put to flight the darkness of sin.

VERS. 4.-- *In secret.* That alms is done in secret which is mingled with no darkness: the light is within, the darkness without. *He seeth in secret.* To see, in God, is to approve. But he approves only those things which are hidden, the things which are without do not please him, neither does he approve them.

[0099B]VERS. 5.-- *And when you pray.* This sentence is joined to what goes before. He had said above: *Take heed that you do not your justice before men;* here he adds: *And when you pray.* He does not forbid to pray, but to be like the hypocrites in praying. *In the corners.* As it were hiders of prayers, and yet in the streets that they may be seen, and by this a fuller glory. Allegorically. He prays in a corner who feigns to pray in secret: and yet in the street, when he catches at fame. The corners of the streets are where a way is led through by the crossing of a way, and makes a crossroads. For it is not wrong to be seen, but to desire to be seen. *They have received.* In these men not only is the true reward emptied out by a depraved intention: but the vice of dissimulation and of mockery against God is increased.

VERS. 6.-- *But thou.* This, simply understood, [0099C] teaches that the vainglory of the world is to be fled. But it seems rather to be enjoined that, the thought of the breast being enclosed and the lips pressed together, one should pray to God. Now the chamber is the secret place of the heart. The door, the carnal sense through which these outward things shamelessly thrust themselves in, and the crowds of phantasms make a din against those who pray. It is little therefore to enter the chamber, if the door stands open to importunate thoughts. But the carnal sense must be resisted, that spiritual prayer may be directed to God out of the inmost parts of the heart. *The door being shut.* The senses being shut, lest the crowds of outward phantasms should meet him. Or he calls the door the love or the fear of this world. For as every good thing is of the fear and love of God, so every evil is of the love and fear of the world. These being shut, that is, taken away, pray.

[0099D] [n: (CHRYSOST.)] What then, sayest thou? ought one not to pray in the church? And very much indeed, but with this will, that thou look upon that one alone who has the power of granting what thou shalt have asked. For God everywhere beholds with what regard thou doest anything.

*The Father.* Whom thou hast within by faith; whence: *With me is prayer to the God of my life [n: (Psal. XLI)]*.

VERS. 7.-- *But praying.* As it is of hypocrites to be shown and to please men, so it is of the Gentiles to use much speaking, from whom also it began. For these give more pains to exercising the tongue than to cleansing the mind: so that they transfer this kind of trifling office even to the bending of God by prayer, thinking that as an orator bends a judge, so they too can bend God.

[0100A] [n: (CHRYSOST.)] If we must pray in few words, why did Luke set forth a parable that we must always pray upon the mountain, etc., *as far as* If indeed both Christ and Paul commanded that prayers be made short, but frequent, at short intervals.

[n: (CASS.)] They (the Fathers) judge it more useful that prayers be short indeed, but very frequent, etc., *as far as* let us avoid by a concise brevity.

*For they think.* Thinking that God is soothed by persuasive words. Or that if he is absent he is called: and that what he does not know he is taught by the windings of words.

VERS. 8.-- *Be not therefore like to them.* For with God the business is not to be done with words, but with things, with the intention of the heart, with a simple affection. Which things when we say, we do not teach him, but we ourselves remember at the time of praying. [0100B] *For the Father knoweth.* Why then do we speak to one who knows? Not that we may make a declaration of our will, but that we may stir up the service of a devout affection.

VERS. 9. *Our Father. [n: (BEDA.)]* Among the other saving and divine admonitions with which he takes counsel for believers, he set forth a form of praying, etc., *as far as* and these are the true adorers, who as Sons by grace adore the Father in spirit and in truth.

No prayer is more spiritual than that which proceeded from the mouth of the Son, who is Truth. *Our Father.* Whom we serve not by fear, but by love of the inheritance. While he is called Father, let us think of adoption, that we may repay to the Father a dutiful affection. While it is said *our,* he is admonished of brotherhood, since the adoption is common to all. Let no one say "mine," which belongs properly to the Son, [0100C] to whom he is Father by nature. Whence elsewhere. *I go to my Father [n: (Joan. VII)]*, specially by nature: and yours, joined by grace. *Our Father is said,* which is common to all, let no one say "mine": which belongs to Christ alone, who is Son by nature; to others is granted the common grace of adoption.

[n: (RAB.)] The noble and the rich man is admonished not to be proud, etc., *as far as* What will he deny to sons, who has already given that he is Father?

[n: (AUG.)] Nowhere is a precept found for the people of Israel, that it should say: *Our Father,* or should pray, etc., *as far as* if they did not stray from his commandments. As is that: *I have begotten sons and exalted them [n: (Isa. I)]* [var: Vulg. Is 1:2 *Filios enutrivi, et exaltavi*, "I have brought up children, and exalted them"], etc

*In the heavens.* The spiritual ones, that we may learn to hasten to the spirituality in which [0100D] he dwells, and may seek heavenly things from him.

*Hallowed be thy name.* The distinction of these seven petitions is to be observed. For since our life is carried on in time and eternal life is hoped for, the former are, etc., *as far as* for liberation makes free men, that is, sons, so that we may say in the spirit of adoption, Abba, Father.

*Amen,* signifies that in all these petitions what is asked is granted by the Lord without doubt, if we do not neglect to keep the compact of the last condition. Whence he adds: *If you shall forgive,* etc. *Hallowed be,* etc. Here we pray for the spirit of wisdom, that we may not, first, in anything depart from the sanctification of the name: but that the name of the Father may be shown in the sons by manners and by life.

[0101A]The name of the Father is in us, who are called sons: which we ask to be hallowed. Not that he himself may be holier, but that he may work in us an increase of his sanctification: for the sanctification of the sons is attributed to his name. So he is said to be hallowed as he is glorified and magnified in us: *Hallowed be,* that is, so as it is holy, let it be held by men: and so let God become known to them, that they may not think anything holier.

VERS.10.-- *Thy kingdom come.* Here the spirit of understanding is asked for, by which the heart is cleansed that God may be seen. The hardness and power of the devil is shut out, and in the future more perfectly, when he shall have made void all principality and power, and the kingdom shall be delivered to God the Father. It fittingly follows, that after the adoption of sons we should ask for the kingdom which is due to sons.

[0101B]The kingdom of God always is: but let it come, that is, let it be made manifest to men by whom, as light by the blind, it is not seen, which no one will be able to be ignorant of, when the Son shall have come to judge. In which the saints also shall reign, as it is said, *Receive the kingdom which is prepared for you [n: (Matth. XXV)]* [var: Vulg. Mt 25:34 *possidete paratum vobis regnum*, "possess the kingdom prepared for you"], etc.

By the spirit of understanding the future kingdom is declared to those entering in, and cleanness of heart is bestowed, through which God, reigning there, shall be seen as he is, where by the spirit of wisdom the seventh sanctification of his name shall be completed. In the perfection of the number six the coming of the kingdom is asked for, that we may all run into the perfect man: then, for those resting in him, may he himself be hallowed in us while we are hallowed in him. His rest we rightly ask to be hallowed in us, that being hallowed in him we may rest perpetually, in which sanctification the peace [0101C] of blessedness is made firm and full wisdom is given.

*Thy will be done.* Here the spirit of counsel is asked for, by which the will of God is sought out, that it may be fulfilled by us.

The will of God on earth as in heaven is governed by the spirit of counsel. We too have need of the spirit of counsel: that the will of God may be directed in us, that we may be able to be merciful in deed. The will of God is always done: but we pray that the liberty of our choice may be joined by grace to his will, which is our sanctification and life everlasting. The will of God is the keeping of his commandments.

*As in heaven.* As in the angels, so in men. Or as in the just, so in sinners converted. Or [0101D] as in Christ, so in the Church. Or as in mind I serve the law of God, so also in the flesh.

According to the spirit we are heaven, according to the flesh we are earth. We pray therefore that as in heaven, that is, in the spirit, so on earth the will may be done: that flesh and spirit may be a spiritual man, of whom it is said: *My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.* Nor is it only prayed that we may will good things, but that the will may be done in us, that we may live to thee, not to ourselves. These three are had more perfectly in the future, but here meanwhile we pray in part, that afterwards they may be had more perfectly. The four following are the safeguards of the present life.

VERS. 11.-- *Bread.* The hunger of justice, that it may attain to fullness, is propped up by the spirit of fortitude. Therefore [0102A] we pray: Give us this day our daily bread: without which we should die of hunger.

Bread is the body of Christ, or the word of God, or God himself, of whom we daily have need, or that which is above all substances. *This is the living bread which came down from heaven [n: (Joan. VI)]* [var: Vulg. Jo 6:51 *Ego sum panis vivus, qui de caelo descendi*, "I am the living bread which came down from heaven"], the sublimity of whose nature is above all substances.

*Our.* Because Christ has been made ours, and God the Father with Christ has given us all things. Therefore we pray that what is ours by gift may daily be given by effect.

*Supersubstantial.* Or daily. Because *they that eat me shall yet hunger [n: (Eccl. XLIV)]*. Here daily, in the fatherland eternal. This bread ought continually to refresh us inwardly by faith and charity: because without it [0102B] no one can live. Or spiritual precepts are called bread, which must always be practised or kept.

VERS. 12.-- *And forgive,* etc. After food he asks pardon of sins, that he who is fed by God may live in God, and may come to eternal life.

When we say: *Forgive us our debts:* we ask for the spirit of knowledge, by which we understand our offences, which without the spirit of knowledge are not understood. For knowledge belongs to the use of temporal things, which is a virtue in avoiding evils and seeking goods, that we may bewail our own contagions and those of others, and may desire good things.

*As.* Behold with what caution we are bound, in which also he bends us mutually to mercy, and promises pardon to those who sin against him, and promises pardon to us and through [0102C] us to others.



## CHAPTER VI. (cont.)

We ought not to deny pardon of a fault; whence: *When you pray, forgive if you have anything against any man: for otherwise your Father will not forgive you your sins.* [var: Vulg. Mc 11:25 *dimittite si quis habetis adversus aliquem : ut et Pater vester, qui in caelis est, dimittat vobis peccata vestra*, "forgive if you have anything against any man: that your Father also, who is in heaven, may forgive you your sins"]

It is granted to demand money back from someone, but we never justly deny pardon to one asking it for the debts of sins.

VERS. 13.-- *And lead us not.* But enlighten us with the spirit of knowledge, that we may know by what evils we are entangled, and we ask that our tears may profit: *Forgive us our debts. And lead us not,* etc. Not that he himself leads in, but because he deserts and permits us to go. Nor indeed does he pray not to be tempted, but not to be overcome even a little. For temptation is necessary for the crown. *And lead us not,* etc., deserting us [0102D] in temptation, do not suffer us to be overcome: even though thou suffer us to be tempted, without which no one is proved.

*But deliver us from evil.* This one petition contains as much as all the foregoing.

That by the spirit of the fear of God all hurtful things within and without may be driven away: and that under poverty we may live blessedly. *But deliver us.* Into that which is not yet, suffer us not to be led, and from that into which we have been led, deliver us: which being done, nothing is to be feared, nothing remains to be prayed for.

*From evil,* from all evil, visible and invisible. This deliverance is daily necessary, since without evil of soul and body there is no living, but it shall be completed in the end, when we shall be immortal and impassible. From the lowest to the highest the ascent is thus made by degrees. From evil, through the spirit of fear, [0103A] we are delivered: thence being delivered we desire to be poor in spirit and in goods, while we say, Lead us not into temptation. We ask for the spirit of piety, that the inward man may grow gentle and become meek, lest he be moved by temptation.

VERS. 14.-- *For if you shall forgive.* He has imposed a form of how we would be judged. Whence for those who pardon there answers before God a confidence of obtaining: but those who exact, the penalty of vengeance or of damnation bites again.

VERS. 15.-- *But if you shall not forgive.* No excuse is left, because everyone shall be judged in the future according to this sentence. From this it is plain that everyone is condemned in his own unbelief.

VERS. 16.-- *When you fast.* After he taught how [0103B] one must pray, he teaches concerning fasting, which again pertains to cleanness of heart, lest it be not simple toward God, while it is carried away to outward things. *Be not made.* He does not forbid the virtue, but the feigned appearance of virtue.

It is good to be sorrowful by fasting for sins unto repentance, and to humble our soul; whence: *A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise [n: (Psal. L)]*. But the sadness that is for praise, he forbids. Whence he does not say simply: Do not fast, but adds: like the hypocrites, sad.

*They drive beyond bounds.* That is, they draw them beyond the bounds of the human condition. As there is boasting from the sheen of garments: so from excessive squalor and leanness. To demolish is as it were to destroy: and to reduce as it were to nothing the comeliness of the countenance. *Their faces.* With mournful filth in [0103C] which also there is boasting: and the more do they deceive under the appearance of religion.

Note that sheep ought not to lay aside their own skins, but to be clothed, if sometimes wolves cover themselves with them.

VERS. 17.-- *Anoint thy head.* Refresh thy mind with spiritual gladness on the days of abstinence: that the odour of love may be fragrant in works of mercy. Wash thy conscience with tears: that it may be clean before God. For the work of mercy does not suffice without a clean conscience: nor this without that. It was the custom among the Palestinians to anoint the head at feasts: therefore anoint thy head, that is, show thyself festive and cheerful: and refresh thy mind with spiritual oil: and seek not praise outwardly for thy fasting. But because thou art thus turned away from the world, rejoice before God: and so shalt thou cleanse thy face, that is, thy heart, from filth: which being removed, [0103D] it will be permitted to see God. *Anoint thy head.* Behold, not yet all things in the New Testament according to the letter. For they would be ridiculous who were smeared with oil in fasting: but of the spirit of his love, in whose sufferings we ought to share, ourselves being to be mortified, the mind ought to be anointed, and not with the oil of flattery: otherwise fastings are vain.

Christ was made an ointment for us: which being poured out through the passion of his death filled his Church with his odour. Therefore we ought not to fast for another's sake: but being poured over with his spirit, mortifying the flesh by abstinence, let us share in his passion. Let us then be anointed with him: that the works of mercy may be heaped up: and charity be poured abroad within: because without him the cup of our fasting is not made drunk with the affection of piety.

[0104A]He fasts to God who mortifies himself for love of him and bestows on another what he withdraws from himself.

VERS. 18.-- *And thy Father.* The Father is within through faith: and rewards deeds done in secret. There therefore must one fast, where he himself may see. And it is necessary that he who fasts should so fast that he may please him whom he carries in his breast.

VERS. 19.-- *Lay not up treasures.* He commands that earthly things be paid out unto cleanness of heart.

VERS 20.-- *But to lay up treasures.* [var: Vulg. Mt 6:20 *Thesaurizate*, imperative, "lay up treasures"] As if: When you fast or do any good work: lay it up there where corruption cannot come.

*In heaven.* That is, place all your hope in heavenly things: walking by faith, embracing charity. *In heaven,* that is, in the spiritual firmament: which does not pass away: [0104B] *Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away.* If therefore the heart is in heaven, it is clean, because heavenly things are clean. But if it is rolled about upon the earth, how is it clean? that is, if it does anything in order to obtain earthly things, how is it clean? For if those things are clean in their own kind, yet the worthier thing grows foul while it is mingled with the lower: as gold with silver, silver with lead.

VERS. 21.-- *For where the treasure is.* If on earth, the heart is below; if in heavenly things, the heart is fixed in Christ.

VERS. 22.-- *The lamp.* He pursues cleanness of heart. As the eye directs the members to work, so do intention and the light of faith direct all the virtues. A lamp is a light in an earthen vessel, so is charity in faith. When faith shall cease, [0104C] charity alone will be the light. From the outward, he teaches the office of the inward man, by the intention of the mind and the light of faith all the virtues are illuminated, that they may render the body lightsome.

Likewise this chapter is of itself unto cleanness of heart, or by reason of the former works which appear openly.

*If the eye be,* etc. If with a pure intention thou doest the good things thou canst, the works are of light, even if it does not so appear to men. If the intention is perverse, whatever is done is depraved, even though it seem right.

The eye is one and simple, namely charity, which now shines in faith as in an earthen vessel.

VERS. 23.-- *But if the eye.* If the intention is not of faith, the whole inward man is dark. Because [0104D] what is not of faith is sin. *Shall be darksome.* Since indeed the intention that follows forms the work. Therefore if the good things which thou doest, because they are done with an evil intention, are darkness, what of those which are of themselves evil, and are done with an evil intention? *If then the light.* The intention with which we do whatever we do, which is known within us, is called light; but the outcome of the thing is uncertain, as when I give or do something to someone I know not whether it turn out to him for good or for evil: and therefore he calls it darkness. He says therefore: If the intention with which thou doest (which is known to thee) is soiled by an appetite for temporal things: how much more the deed itself, whose outcome is doubtful? because even if it turn out well for another, what thou doest not with a good intention will profit thee nothing: because it is imputed to thee how thou hast done it, not how it has turned out for him.

[0105A]VERS. 24.-- *No man can,* etc. As if: you will not be able to do good things before the eyes of men, and by these to please God. Not to lay up treasure at once in heaven and on earth, nor to serve both vices and virtues. Whatever thou doest, either of the love of God, or of the servitude of the devil.

Since the kingdom of God and of the devil are at variance among themselves, no one can serve as a soldier in both at once: whence they who are baptized renounce the devil and his works.

*For either he will hate the one.* There is nothing between. For whatever thou doest, either of the love of God, or of the servitude of the devil.

[n: (AUG.)] For the devil is always to be held in hatred: but God, etc., *as far as* but they despise, overcome by their own concupiscence and by diabolical persuasion.

*Or he will sustain the one. [n: (ID.)]* Not indeed that he loves him: [0105B] for no one loves the devil, but being entangled by his own cupidity, etc., *as far as* even if he love not him whose handmaid he loves.

*He will despise the other.* Not indeed that he will hate him: for no one's conscience can hate God, which the same Augustine retracted, saying: I do not see that it ought to have been said. For there are many of whom it is written: *The pride of them that hate thee [n: (Psal. III)]*, etc.

*And mammon.* Mammon, in the Syrian tongue, riches, to serve which is to deny God. He does not say to have: which is lawful to be done so that one may dispense it well, but to serve, which belongs to the covetous. This is said to be the name of a demon who presides over riches, not because they are in his dominion: but because he uses these for deceiving, ensnaring men in the nets of riches.

[0105C]VERS. 25.-- *Therefore I say to you,* etc. *Because you cannot serve God and mammon.* Be not solicitous, which is to serve riches. He has enjoined contempt of the world and confidence in things to come throughout the whole sermon, since he commanded both to bear evils and not to avenge, and to love enemies, and to flee human glory. Now he wishes to confirm it through faith in the hope of eternal things, because there are many whom the love of present things and despair of things to come make torpid.

In the sweat of the face bread is got ready, but labour is to be exercised, solicitude is to be removed, which disturbs the mind: while it fears lest either the things possessed perish or the things laboured for do not come to hand.

*Your soul.* That is, to the animal nature to which these things are necessary. Commit your whole hope to God, because you can acquire or retain nothing, [0105D] except what he has decreed.

Soul is here put for life, which is sustained by food, as there: *He that loveth his soul shall lose it [n: (Joan. XII)]*.

The animal nature is nourished by food: and is here put for life: it lives with the cattle. And he who loses it for Christ's sake shall find it spiritual unto life everlasting.

*Is not the soul?* etc. Not life for the sake of food, nor the body for the sake of raiment, but the contrary. Therefore let not the mind be solicitous, that it may receive that for whose sake it was created.

As if he should say: He who gave the greater, that is, life and body, will give also the lesser, that is, food and clothing. [0106A] Let no one doubt in these promises of the truth: Let man be what he ought to be, and forthwith all things are added to him for whose sake they were made.

VERS. 26.-- *Behold.* This concerning food. The saints are deservedly compared to birds, because they seek heaven, and some are so far removed from the world that they now do nothing on earth, but by contemplation alone already dwell in heaven. Of whom it is said: *Who are these that fly as clouds? [n: (Isa. LX)]*, etc.

These examples do not forbid providence, that it should not labour, but solicitude, that your whole confidence may be in God, since even the birds live without care.

*And your Father.* He heightens and confirms the confidence of sons: because if the goodness of the Father extends itself even to those things, how much more to the sons of adoption?

[0106B]VERS. 27.-- *And which of you,* etc. But leave to him the care of governing the body, who made it come to this measure.



## CHAPTER VI. (cont.)

VERS. 28.-- *And for raiment.* [var: Vulg. Mt 6:28 *Et de vestimento*, singular] Not that this, to labour and to provide, is not fitting, but all solicitude must be cast away, and hope must be had in God. *Consider the lilies of the field.* He confirms by a sufficiently fitting example the exhortation concerning clothing.

VERS. 29.-- *That not even Solomon,* etc. What purple of kings, what painting of weaving-women can be compared to flowers? The colour itself is called the covering of the flowers, as we say: a redness has covered that man.

VERS. 30.-- *For if the grass of the field.* [var: Vulg. Mt 6:30 *Si autem foenum agri*, "But if the grass of the field"] If those things which are for the use of time only, and quickly falling, shall be burnt with fire, God adorns them so beautifully.

[0106C]"Tomorrow" is put for the future in the Scriptures, Jacob saying: *My justice shall hear me tomorrow [n: (Gen. XXX)]* [var: Vulg. Gn 30:33 *Respondebitque mihi cras justitia mea*, "And my justice shall answer for me tomorrow"].

*Is cast into the oven.* Other books have: into the fire, or into a heap which has the appearance of an oven. *How much more you,* namely, will he clothe; and therefore all confidence is to be had in him; but if we are not confident even about these things, how do we hope for things invisible? Very small is the faith which is not certain even about the least things. Therefore he both presses upon us confidence about eternal things, and condemns unbelief. *Of little faith.* Whosoever doubts in any promise, is of little faith, and the more he doubts, the less he finds those things for which he was solicitous.

VERS. 31.-- *Be not therefore solicitous,* etc. He more fully inculcates [0106D] and turns over what he taught from the beginning of the sermon, that we should live without solicitude. *Be not,* etc. Here those seem to be reproved who, despising the common food or clothing, seek for themselves foods or garments more sumptuous or more austere than those among whom they live. *To be solicitous.* Solicitude chokes the word of God, that it may not bear fruit, and makes a man like a Gentile, that is, unbelieving.

VERS. 32.-- *For all these things.* What more then has he than a Gentile: whose unbelief makes the mind anxious, and wearies it with the cares of this life? *The Gentiles.* Who have no care about things to come, but it belongs to sons to seek the kingdom. *For he knoweth.* These things are provided by God, who knows that they are necessary for us on his way. *Your Father.* Thus he makes sons secure concerning [0107A] the goodness and providence of the Father, that is, without care.

VERS. 33.-- *Seek therefore.* Here he plainly shows that these things are not to be sought as our goods, although they are necessary. But the kingdom of God is to be sought, and in it our end is to be placed, for whose sake we should do all things: for example: Let us eat that we may preach the Gospel, we do not preach the Gospel that we may eat. When he says "first," he signifies that this is later, not in time, but in dignity. For that is to be sought, this is necessary for the sake of that: therefore seek first the kingdom of God, that is, set it before all other things.

*And all these things.* Because all things are the sons': and therefore all these things shall be added, even to those who do not seek them, from whom if they are withdrawn, it is for a trial; if [0107B] they are given, it is for thanksgiving; because all things work together unto good.

VERS. 34.-- *Solicitous.* By fear, by grief, and by the anxiety of cares, which disturb the mind.

*For the morrow. [n: (AUG.)]* For the future, concerning present things he grants it: whence the Apostle: *Night and day we worked, that we might not burden any man [n: (I Thes. II)]* [var: Vulg. 1Thes 2:9 *nocte ac die operantes, ne quem vestrum gravaremus*, "working night and day, that we might not burden any of you"]. Concerning things to come, which the divine ordering provides for, it is not fitting, etc., *as far as* because he who gave this precept, to whom angels ministered, in order that this example might be given had purses: whence he might supply the things necessary for their uses, of which Judas was the keeper.

*The day.* Not that which the Lord made, but that which Job and Jeremias cursed, namely that which the devil found. *It sufficeth.* And because minds are overwhelmed by present care, the malice of God [cj: *Dei*; read *diei*, "of the day"] ought not to be made to sprout.



## CHAPTER VII.

[0107C]

VERS. 1.-- *Judge not.* Of doubtful matters, since judgment is passed on manifest ones, and not on those of which it is uncertain with what mind they are done: of which no one judges without danger.

Rash judgment is when men judge in matters not committed to them, whether it be of manifest things or of hidden ones. Now judgment is committed either to the masters of the Church or to the princes of the earth. These therefore, if they judge of manifest things, those namely which are proved or confessed, do not judge rashly; but if of uncertain things, they judge rashly: these judgments he forbids.

VERS. 2.-- *For with what.* As if he were to say: In what will thou hast done well, in that same shalt thou be set free; and in what [0107D] ill, in that same shalt thou be punished. For the matter here concerns those things in which we either offend by judging rashly, or are excused by acting rightly; and therefore he adds: *With what measure.* And justly, those whose will had no end of sinning, although they sinned with an end, have no end of vengeance; and those whose judgment was without mercy shall be judged without mercy.

*With what measure.* It can be that in this same measure, in which one thing has been measured out, wheat for instance, another should be measured, barley for instance: and another quantity too, as if one bushel of the one, a hundred of the other. So God does, and not unjustly, that for them [it be] unto eternity.

And the very infamy, or the evil which thou hast brought, is the cause why thou incurrest the punishment that is due.

[0108A]Justly do those who wish to enjoy sin eternally find also an eternal punishment: whose will had no end of sinning, nor shall it have an end of being tormented.

VERS. 3.-- *And why seest thou.* Behold the moderation of judgment, and let not one who is himself forestalled by greater faults judge another for lesser ones. For many, forestalled by greater faults, would rather find fault with lighter ones in a brother and condemn them than amend them. As if, being full of hatred or envy or malice, they should condemn in him that wherein anger offends; which anger is as a mote, and hatred as a beam. One who is angry with another sometimes wishes him to be corrected; he who hates cannot wish this: and therefore it is called impossible that he should take away the mote from his brother who carries a beam; first therefore the beam of hatred, of envy, of dissimulation and of all malice must be cast away, so that we may thus mercifully, with regard to God, not to ourselves, rebuke [0108B] our brother: so that, whether the correction profit him or not, we at any rate may be secure concerning the singleness of our own eye.

Scarcely is anyone found free from this vice, since each man, favouring his own, easily reprehends what is another's: and, bearing another's faults more heavily than his own, he assumes the authority of reproving without the example of his own amendment.

Salvation, in that they judge rashly they have a beam in the eye.

VERS. 4.-- *Or how sayest thou to thy brother.* That is, thou wilt not be able to amend the lesser thing (anger, for instance) in thy brother, until thou hast driven the greater, that is hatred, or envy, out of thy own heart.

VERS. 5.-- *Thou hypocrite, cast out.* For these men take it upon themselves out of hatred and spite to accuse everything, and wish to seem counsellors without the example of their own amendment. For [0108C] he is no fit teacher to heal another who has not yet healed himself.

VERS. 6.-- *Give not that which is holy,* etc. The eye being cleansed, the stewards of the Church can chastise others, but not give what is holy to dogs; for as it is dangerous to hide it, so it is prodigal to give it to dogs. To such men mystical things are not to be opened, but the holy of holies is to be covered with a veil: yet things more open, and as it were commoner, may be spoken. *Give not.* The same thing is called both what is holy and a pearl, that is, the Gospel and the sacraments of the Church. *That which is holy,* because by nature inviolable, and it ought not to be corrupted by anyone. *A pearl,* which lies hidden in secret: and out of the figures, as out of opened shells, is drawn a precious gem which cannot be corrupted. Dogs indeed are those who bark against it and tear in pieces [0108D] what is whole; swine, those who set it at nought and trample it: or dogs are those returned to their vomit, swine those not yet converted, but wallowing in the mire of the vices.

*And turning upon you.* Lest perchance, hearing yet something further, they rend, not the pearls, which they trample, but you, by their indignation. For it cannot easily be found what would be pleasing to such men.

VERS. 7.-- *Ask.* By these steps the way, the truth, and the life are granted to those who strive lawfully: Christ is the way by which one walks, the truth by which he is found, the door at which one knocks, that we may enter to him through him.

[n: (AUG.)] Laboriously indeed did I think it must be set forth how these three differ among themselves, but far better, etc., [0109A] *as far as* for he did not say, to those asking, and seeking, and knocking.

VERS. 8.-- *For every one,* etc. That he may furnish constancy in persevering, diligence in seeking, confidence in obtaining, he adds. *Every one,* etc. Above he taught what we should ask, namely the kingdom. Here, confidence, that we may ask hesitating in nothing. He does not deny himself to those who ask, who freely offered himself to those who did not ask: and those who seek shall find him who granted to those who did not seek that they should find, and to those who knock he will open, who cries: *Behold, I stand at the door and knock [n: (Apoc. III)]*.

VERS. 9.-- *Or what man.* He explains what is to be asked, and from human kindness toward children he commends the Father's care toward us. To those who ask for Christ with right faith there is given no stone of stumbling, nor hardness [0109B] of heart. So if you ask your father for charity, without which all else is nothing, as without bread the table is destitute, to which hardness of heart is contrary.

VERS. 10.-- *If he ask a fish.* By the fish, the faith which is nourished beneath the streams of the Holy Spirit.

By the fish he means faith in things invisible: either because of the water of baptism, or because it is taken out of invisible places, or because it is not broken by the waves of this world. In Luke's Gospel there follows the comparison of the egg and the scorpion. In the egg hope also is understood, because in it the young is not yet brought through; but by cherishing it is hoped for. In the scorpion, whose sting is to be feared behind, is understood the contrary of hope, namely to look backward, whereas hope ought to stretch itself forward.

VERS. 11.-- *If you then.* Since fathers [0109C] bestow good things upon their children, therefore much more will our Father, who is incomparably good, give good things to the children who ask him. *You know how to give good things.* Good according to the judgment of those who hold them for good, although in the nature of things they too are good, and pertain to this present life, which an evil man does not give of his own. *For the earth is the Lord's [n: (Psal. XXIII)]*, etc. Or the apostles are called evil, as regards themselves in comparison with God, who alone is good, from whom all are good. *Will give good things.* That is, the Holy Spirit. Or good things, namely eternal ones, which are not given save to sons. *To them that ask him.* The distributor of all spiritual goods, that the works of charity may be fulfilled.

VERS. 12.-- *All things therefore,* etc. Because to love one who loves is a thing of nature; but that one who does not love should be constrained by benefits to love, is of Christ's perfection. When he had commanded us first, [0109D] to do to others what we would wish to be done to us, he at once builds up the same sense, saying: *All things therefore whatsoever,* etc., that is, the good things which you wish to receive from others, do the same to them, that the charity of the neighbour may be fulfilled, which without love cannot rightly be perfected.
