And therefore he adds: *This is the law and the prophets,* etc.; because neither is God loved without the neighbour, nor the neighbour without God, since the neighbour is not to be judged out of hatred or out of envy: therefore with what charity you would wish to be admonished, do to others. *That men should do to you.* Because he adds "men", he speaks only of the love of the neighbour. Whence neither does he subjoin "the whole law", but leaves aside what belongs to the love of God. But if he had said: All things whatsoever you wish to be done to you, do to others: he would have embraced both, in which [0110A] is the whole law, for the salvation of men it is written in the prophets and in the law.

VERS. 13.-- *Enter ye.* Although it be hard that thou shouldst do to others what thou wishest to be done to thee, yet so it must be done that we may enter. *By the narrow gate.* The narrow one is sought, and is not found by all. Nor do all who find it enter by it, because, taken captive by the world, they go back. *And broad.* Although they do not seek this one, yet all find it, because they were born in it. Pleasure, like an importunate harlot, invites all by her delights: and therefore many enter by it.

VERS. 14.-- *How narrow.* It is narrow enough to pass by all things, to love one alone, to seek one, to knock daily at one, not to court prosperity, not to fear adversity. *And few.* If few find it, [0110B] fewer strive to enter by it. No one enters without labour, and without purity of mind.

VERS. 15.-- *Beware.* When he had said that the narrow way is found by few, lest perchance his own should be entangled in the errors of the pseudo-prophets, he added: Beware: *Beware.* What above he called the broad gate, he more openly calls false prophets. *Beware.* Although this may be understood of all who show one thing in dress and speech and another in deed; yet it is especially of heretics, who, covered with a certain garment of piety, are ravening wolves with a venomous mind and an intent to harm, either outwardly by persecuting, if opportunity be given, or inwardly by corrupting.

*To you in the clothing of sheep.* In the sight of men they are like ministers of justice while they fast, pray, give alms: but these are not their fruits, because [0110C] it is reckoned to them for a vice.

*By their fruits. [n: (HIER.)]* Not by the vesture, but by the works, which is of things manifest, etc., *as far as* but the sheep ought not to lay aside their fleeces, even if wolves sometimes cover themselves with them.

VERS. 16.-- *Do they gather.* Allegorically. Thorns and thistles are the heretics, from whom no one of the wise will be able to find holiness or truth: rather they tear and bloody those who come near. Or thorns and thistles are the cares of the world, and the prickings of the vices. The grape and the fig are the sweetness of the new manner of life, for which Christ hungers in us, and the fervour of love, which gladdens the heart of man. Not from thorns and thistles, therefore, come the grape and the fig: because a mind still pressed down by the habit of the old man can feign, not bear, the fruits [0110D] of the new man. But if sometimes the words or deeds of evil men profit the good, the evil do not do this, but it comes about from them by the counsel of God: because it is not their fruit, but the vine's, which sometimes runs over upon the thorns. But the cluster is to be plucked, the thorn avoided. Christ is the vine. His own are the branches which bear the grapes, that is, the works of the spirit, which make the mind drunk.

VERS. 17.-- *So every tree.* That is, according to the aforesaid impossibility: because from an evil root the fruit of sweetness cannot break forth. Good fruits are to be looked for from a good tree. A tree good or evil is not nature, which in all things was created good by God, but the will, good or evil. The fruits are the works, which can neither be good works of an evil will, nor [0111A] evil works of a good will. The fruits of a good tree are joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, etc.; which fruits none but a good will brings forth. So on the contrary an evil intention nourishes evil ones.

VERS. 18.-- *A good tree cannot.* He does not say: An evil tree cannot become good, or a good one evil; for Paul from a persecutor was made an apostle, and, the soul's nature remaining whole, it is corrupted by the affection of the will, or is changed for the better.

The will of each man is a tree good or evil. And as a tree is rooted in the earth, so is the will in the soul.

The fruits of an evil tree are the works of the flesh, namely unclean fornication, luxury.

VERS. 19.-- *Every tree.* By this sentence he condemns hypocrites [0111B] and pseudo-prophets, and what he taught above concerning cleanness of heart he confirms by this example, that no one receives good fruit from an evil intention, nor reaps from a good one anything but good.



## CHAPTER VII. (cont.)

VERS. 20.-- *Therefore by their fruits.* As if he should say: Beware of false prophets, and know them by their fruits.

VERS. 21.-- *Not every one that saith.* As those are to be guarded against who have the appearance of a good life because of a doctrine of wickedness, so here on the contrary are those who, though they be of entire faith and doctrine, live basely. For both are needful, that the work be approved by the word, and the word by the works.

*That saith: Lord, Lord.* The road of the kingdom of God is obedience, not the calling of a name. This is not that [0111C] saying truly and properly, where the utterance is at variance with the will. Of which the Apostle says: *No man can say: Lord Jesus, but in the Holy Ghost [n: (I Cor. XII)]*.

VERS. 22.-- *Many will say.* But most of all are those to be guarded against who, for the name of Christ, have even miracles, and although the Lord wrought these for the sake of unbelievers, yet he warned us not to be deceived by such men: thinking that invisible wisdom is there where there is a visible miracle; whence he adds: *Many will say.* How clean and single an eye then is needed, that the way of wisdom may be found amid so many deceptions.

VERS. 23.-- *I never knew you.* The light does not know the darkness, that is, it does not look upon it, since if it looked upon it, it would not be darkness. *You that work iniquity.* Not "who have worked", lest he take away repentance, but "who work" at the judgment; [0111D] although you have not the power of sinning, yet you have the desire.

VERS. 24.-- *Every one therefore.* As if he should say: All the foregoing must be well kept, because he who keeps them shall be likened to Christ; he who keeps them not, to the devil. *But he who,* which things were delivered on the mount: this he says in order to show that the sermon delivered on the mount is perfect in all the precepts by which the Christian life is formed. *Shall be likened.* Because, as Christ out of various persons builds up one Church, instructs it, rules it, being about to dedicate it unto eternal life, so this man by various virtues builds for himself a perpetual dwelling, and in the dedication to come will rejoice with Christ. *To a man.* To him who says: As a wise architect, I have laid the foundation in Christ. [0112A] *Who built.* He builds in Christ who does what he hears from him. *Upon a rock.* From which Peter received his name, for the firmness of his faith, that is, he built the Church upon himself.

VERS. 25.-- *And there came down.* In three ways the devil assails: by the concupiscence of the flesh, by the outward delights of the world, or by himself, when he looses upon all the wind of his impulsions. *The rain.* Concupiscence, by which each man is tempted, which softens the sense, the rigour of faith, which if it does not prevail, greater floods come on.

VERS. 26.-- *Who heareth these my words,* etc., outwardly. And therefore he has no excuse, but great is his ruin: because he despised the warnings of salvation. *To a foolish man.* Of whom it is said: *An enemy hath done this, whose* works are all unstable, and lie open to ruin. *Upon the sand.* [0112B] Of whatever sort the things be that are founded upon the concupiscence of the vices, they shall not stand.

VERS. 27.-- *And it fell, and great was the ruin thereof.* Every conscience which does not remain fixed in God by hope has no strength to stand in temptations; and it is driven the further, the more it is severed from the things above in those things which are of the world: and truly all who are evil, or feignedly good, become worse when any temptation presses upon them.

VERS. 28.-- *The crowds.* Either some in the crowd, because unbelievers, or rather all, [wondered] at the excellence of his wisdom.



## CHAPTER VIII.

VERS. 1.-- *And when he was come down.* After the Lord's descent from the mountain, etc., *as far as* he shows [0112C] after how great an interval of time. *And when he was come down.* According to Luke, and in a level place, he had delivered to him the discourse which perhaps he had already held above. *There followed him.* Some for charity's sake, some for doctrine's, some for wonder and for healing.

VERS. 2.-- *Adored him, saying: Lord.* Before he asked, he showed the worship due to divinity. *If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.* Concerning the will I am in doubt, not as one incredulous of his mercy; but, as one conscious of my own foulness, I do not presume.

VERS. 3.-- *Stretching forth.* After the discourse he works miracles also, by which the discourse is confirmed with the hearers. *He touched him.* Not because he could heal without touch, but that he might show himself not subject to the law, but the Lord of the law, [0112D] who fears no contagion. *He touched him.* For humanity's sake, that he might teach us to despise no one for any defilement of the body. It appears that grace, which heals him, is above the law (which shuts out the leper); as he says: *I am not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil,* etc. *I will.* He healed in that same manner in which he had been besought, then he commands: *Be thou made clean.* Behold his power.

VERS. 4.-- *See, tell no man,* etc. He bade him keep silence, nor yet could he keep silence. Not that he willed something and could not do it, but he gives an example, that his own should wish to lie hidden in the great things they do: yet that they may profit others, they are made known against their will. *Tell no man [n: (Marc. I)]*. Yet Mark, where he says that he preached this, [says] that he was as it were made an Evangelist. *Go.* He sends him to the priests for humility's sake, [0113A] that he may render honour to the priests, to whom the law bids the cleansed offer gifts, and that seeing they may believe him: or, if they do not believe, that they may be without excuse, and lest he should seem to break the law. *Show thyself to the priest.* That the priest may understand that he was healed not by the ordinance of the law, but by the grace of God above the law. *Offer,* etc. Because I do not destroy the law, because the true sacrifice has not yet begun. *For a testimony.* That is, let them believe the Lord, if the leprosy of impiety depart. *For a testimony.* Of the spiritual healing, the spiritual gift to be offered is the man himself.

VERS. 7.-- *I will come and heal him. And the centurion, making answer, said,* etc. Great humility, etc., *as far as* he might be thought to go bodily because of a weakness of strength.

VERS. 8.-- *I am not worthy.* Because of the consciousness [0113B] of his Gentile life, he fears rather to be burdened by his presence than to be helped, for although he was endowed with faith, he was not yet steeped in the sacraments. But what our infirmity does not even presume, grace knows how to give.

VERS. 9.-- *For I also,* etc. If I, a man, etc., *as far as* as Cornelius is called *a just man and one that feareth God [n: (Act. X)]*.

VERS. 11.-- *From the east and the west they shall come and shall sit down.* Or the east means those who, being enlightened, straightway pass over; the west, those who bear sufferings even unto death. By these two quarters of the world, out of which the Gentiles were to be called, they are designated.

VERS. 12.-- *But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out.* Because in this world they enjoy the benefits of God; according to that word: *He raineth upon the just and the unjust.* Now they are seen in [0113C] the face of the Lord, but then not at all. *Into the exterior darkness.* Because they shall be driven forth from the Lord, etc., *as far as* he repents of what he obstinately did amiss. *Weeping.* By this is shown the greatness of the torments. By the weeping, the torment of the soul; by the gnashing of teeth, that of the body.

VERS. 14.-- *And when he was come,* etc. When this was done Matthew has not expressed, etc., *as far as* to suggest to his memory the things to be narrated. *And sick of a fever.* Fever is said in Greek, heat in Latin: and if at any time this affliction makes one tremble, it belongs to human nature.

VERS. 15.-- *And he touched,* etc. Luke says that they besought him, etc., *as far as* as *Who can understand sins: from my secret sins cleanse me [n: (Psal. VIII)]*. *And she arose,* etc. [0113D] It is natural for the fevered to grow faint when health begins, etc., *as far as* she ministers in the spirit.

VERS. 16.-- *And when evening was come,* etc. The setting of the sun is the death of Christ, through which he healed more demoniacs than, living before in the flesh, he had healed sick men.

VERS. 18.-- *And Jesus seeing.* It is manifest that it is another day, etc., *as far as* that we may pass over the bitter waves of the world.

VERS. 19.-- *And there came.* That Matthew says this was done when he bade them go across the strait: but Luke *as they walked in the way:* is not contrary: because they walked in the way that they might come to the strait. *Master.* As though he were one of many. And he himself was a man of letters, not a spiritual hearer. *Master.* He did not say [0114A] Lord, but Master: reckoning him one among many masters.

VERS. 20.-- *The foxes have holes.* As if he should say: Why me, for the gains of the world, etc., *as far as* there is no place for the divinity of Christ. *But the Son of man hath not,* etc. Although men call him the Son of God, he himself calls himself the Son of man, for humility's sake.

VERS. 21.-- *And another.* Note that this man was called by Jesus. *Lord.* He who thrust himself forward calls him Master, like the puffed-up Pharisee, the other, who was received, humbly calls him Lord, like the publican.

VERS. 22.-- *Their dead.* Those who went out in fault, as they themselves live with fault. To bury the dead is to cherish sinners in their sin.

[0114B]VERS. 23.-- *And when he went up.* He who did great things on land passes over to the sea, that he may do them there also, and appear Lord of land and sea.

VERS. 24.-- *Behold a commotion.* The tempest did not arise of itself, but at his command: that the disciples might fear the more and entreat him: and that to those entreating he might show his power. *He was asleep.* The Lord sleeps in us, that is, faith in the Lord, when we act more negligently, and therefore comes the tempest. But if faith rises again, he commands the winds and the waves.

VERS. 25. *They awaked him.* First, Jesus must be roused in tribulations by prayers, that afterwards, rising unto rebuke, he may command the winds and the sea, and there may be a great calm.

VERS. 26.-- *O ye of little faith,* etc. If you have known him powerful [0114C] on land, why do you not believe him so on the sea also? He who believes little is reproved: he who believes nothing is despised. *He commanded,* etc. That which is commanded feels him who commands. Note that every creature feels its Creator. The things which are insensible with us are to him things that feel.

VERS. 27.-- *What manner of man is this,* etc. [n: (ORIG.)] What manner of man is this, greater than Moses, etc., *as far as* they have no hearing, they obey.

VERS. 28. *Into the country of the Gerazenes.* Geraza is a city of Arabia, etc., *as far as* visited by Christ through his preachers. *Two having demons.* Mark and Luke say one, etc., *as far as* they showed the foulness of their bodies. *Exceeding fierce.* Mark says that no one now [could bind] the demoniac, etc., *as far as* they assail any who would pass.

VERS. 29.-- *Jesus, Son of God. [n: (HILAR.)]* They are to be believed rather to have suspected [0114D] than to have known. *[n: (AMBR.)] Jesus, Son of God.* He became known to them just so far as he willed, etc., *as far as* what they saw in him, they did not believe. *Before the time.* For they knew that there would be for them at the judgment of God, etc., *as far as* for there were two thousand, as Mark says. *To torment us.* The presence of Christ is a torture to them; or, they are tormented while they are cast out of the bodies in whose torture they took delight, just as the presence of God is the refreshment of the angels.

VERS. 31.-- *Send us.* Note that they can far less harm men by their own power, who cannot do so even to beasts. Unless a man live after the manner of a swine, the devil receives no power over him, save perhaps for his testing.

VERS. 32.-- *And behold with great violence.* [var: Vulg. Mt 8:32 *et ecce impetu abiit totus grex*, without *magno*] Man is worthier than beasts, [0115A] since for the salvation of two men two thousand swine perished. The people of the Gentiles being set free, unbelievers practise their evil rites in hidden places: sunk in blind and deep curiosity.

VERS. 33.-- *And the keepers fled.* Because certain leaders even of the impious, though they flee the faith of Christ, yet do not cease to proclaim his power in wonder.

VERS. 34.-- *Went out to meet him. [n: (BED.)]* Those coming forth signify certain men bound by habit, who indeed admire and venerate the law of Christ, but are unwilling to suffer it: whence they beg him to pass on. *And they found the man* (as Luke says) *clothed and in his right mind, sitting at the feet of Jesus [n: (Luc. VIII)]*. *They besought him.* They beseech him not out of pride, out of humility judging themselves unworthy, as Peter did, [0115B] and the widow in the case of Elias. They feared lest the presence of his holiness should destroy them because of their sins, as it had destroyed the swine.



## CHAPTER IX.

VERS. 1.-- *Into the city.* Lest thou think this to be Nazareth, etc., *as far as* Capharnaum, as it were the metropolis.

VERS. 2.-- *They offered.* They are the teachers, who lift men up and offer them to Christ by admonishing and by interceding. *Faith.* How much a man's own faith avails with God, with whom another's so availed that he healed the man within and without. *Be of good heart, son, they are forgiven thee.* Luke says: Man, etc., *as far as* taking away the cause of the disease, he afterwards heals the body.

VERS. 5.-- *Which is.* Note that infirmities sometimes [0115C] come about on account of sins, etc., *as far as* whence: *The Lord shall crush them with a double crushing. [n: (BED.)] Which is easier,* [var: Vulg. Jer 17:18 *duplici contritione contere eos*, an imperative with no subject: "crush thou them"] but since you do not believe this spiritual thing, let it be proved by a visible sign, which is agreed to be of no less power, so that in the Son of man you may recognize the hidden power of majesty, which can forgive sins as God.

VERS. 6.-- *Then said he to the man sick of the palsy.* Behold, by the remission of the penalty understand the forgiveness of the fault. *Arise.* To arise is to draw the soul away from carnal desires. To take up the bed is to lift the flesh from earthly desires to the will of the spirit. To go home is to return to paradise, or to the inward keeping of oneself, lest one sin again. *Take up thy bed and go into thy house.* That what was the witness of infirmity [0115D] may be the proof of health.

VERS. 7.-- *And he arose.* Great is the power, where without delay healing accompanies the command. Whence deservedly those who were present, leaving their blasphemies and amazed, are turned to the praise of so great majesty.

VERS. 9.-- *He saw a man.* Here it seems more probable that he is recording things passed over, since he chose the twelve before the sermon. *In the custom-house.* Τέλος in Greek, in Latin a toll. Matthew in Hebrew is in Latin "given", who received so great a gift of grace: Levi, "added" or "taken up", because the divine election took him up and added him to the number of the apostles. *Matthew.* The other Evangelists, out of modesty, etc., *as far as* the aforesaid discourse was. *Rising up. [n: (BED.)]* Luke says more fully: [0116A] leaving all things, he followed him as much in body as in mind. Led not by levity, but drawn by the truth of the works and by the divine power working within, a perfect obedience and a perfect renunciation, he left his gains also, eager to follow Christ.

VERS. 10.-- *In the house.* He does not say whose, but Luke expresses it, etc., *as far as* is shown by the conversion of the penitent. *Behold many publicans.* A good omen: already by his example many are converted. Already he draws many after him, being about to be an Apostle and teacher of the Gentiles. *[n: (HIER.)] With publicans and sinners.* Tertullian says these were heathen, etc., *as far as* he commanded: *Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles. Sinners coming sat down.* Penitents, by Matthew's example, hoping for pardon: whence Mark says here: *that many followed [0116B] him [n: (Marc. II)]*.

VERS. 11.-- *Why with publicans.* Every question, etc., *as far as* and all that he did serves for salvation.

VERS. 12.-- *But Jesus hearing it, said.* He both strengthens further in faith the penitents he has received, and provokes the proud to the grace of humility and of mercy. *They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill.* Christ is the physician, etc., *as far as* they receive the word of God, they cannot hunger.

VERS. 13.-- *And going, say ye.* [var: Vulg. Mt 9:13 *discite*, "learn"] To those swelling with a false righteousness he gives counsel of correction, etc., *as far as* by the sheep, and the drachma, and the two sons. *For I am not come to call the just.* Were not Nathanael, and Peter, and Andrew, etc., *as far as* they no longer seem just to themselves.

[0116C]VERS. 14.-- *But thy disciples do not fast.* John, Mark and Luke, etc., *as far as* thou mayest understand the grace and the power.

VERS. 15.-- *Can they.* As if he should say: You are about to do so, that mourning, etc., *as far as* but from all earthly things. *To mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them.* By this word he expresses that fast, etc., *as far as* afterwards they shall fast, they shall not mourn. *And then they shall fast.* Grief for the bridegroom's absence was wanting neither in the fathers before the incarnation, nor after the passion, save for so long as he lived in the flesh with the disciples. *They shall fast.* From the love of the world, not only from foods. For since the spiritual fast is a part of the new life, it does not yet befit those who in other respects are given over to the old life.

VERS. 16.-- *And no man.* As if he should say: The carnal, [0116D] not yet made firm by faith in the passion and the resurrection, etc., *as far as* it does not suit that very oldness. *For it taketh away.* That is, the perfection of the new life, which is one, is divided, and from the old is taken away the faith which it has, to which the perfection of the new was owed.

VERS. 17.-- *Neither do they put.* He compares those same disciples to old bottles, etc., *as far as* we are inwardly renewed in newness of understanding.

VERS. 18.-- *Behold a certain ruler came up.* Mark and Luke call him a ruler of the synagogue, etc., *as far as* he began to hope for a remedy and to seek it.

VERS. 20.-- *A woman who.* The salvation prepared for the Jews the Gentile world snatched beforehand by a sure hope. *Twelve years.* For twelve years she had an issue, as that daughter also had grown [0117A] to twelve: because from the time when the Synagogue began to serve God, the Gentile world began to be defiled with idolatry and sin. *She came near.* She believed, she spoke, because by these three, by faith and by work, all salvation is gained.

VERS. 21.-- *If I shall touch.* The hem, not the garment. Because she did not see the Lord in the flesh, but received the word of the incarnation through the apostles. Blessed is he who touches by faith even the outermost part of the word.

VERS. 22.-- *Be of good heart, daughter.* She who asked did indeed believe, but he impresses upon her strength and perseverance in faith.

VERS. 23.-- *He had seen.* The minstrels are those singing a mournful song. These are the masters soothing their subjects by their own grief, and the crowd of the Jews kicking against the doctrine of Christ. *And the crowd.* Because the Synagogue the joy of the Lord's indwelling, etc., [0117B] *as far as* it was obedient in the receiving.

VERS. 24.-- *She is not.* To you she is dead. But to God, who can raise her up, she sleeps, as much in soul as in body.

VERS. 25.-- *And when the crowd was put forth.* That is, when the mockers had been rejected, he entered into the minds of the elect. *And he took her hand.* Unless first the hand of the Jews, etc., *as far as* can be blotted out by secret penance.

VERS. 27.-- *As he passed.* That is, from the ruler's house into thy house. The ruler's house is the Synagogue, his own house is the heavenly Jerusalem. *Two blind men,* etc. Two blind men, two ignorant peoples, etc., *as far as* the same deed, but another like it.

VERS. 32.-- *A man.* He signifies the Gentile people: or the whole race of men, which, being led by preaching [0117C] to Christ, and idolatry being taken away, confessed Christ. Κωφὸς is the more usual Greek word, but yet they say indifferently both dumb and deaf.

VERS. 34.-- *But the Pharisees.* In the Pharisees the unbelief of the Jews is signified.



## CHAPTER X.

VERS. 1.-- *And having called together.* From the healing of Peter's mother-in-law, etc., *as far as* the centurion's servant healed. *Twelve.* These are the labourers who were to be sent, and who were to call the quarters of the four-square world to faith in the Trinity. That their preaching might have the weight of authority, power is given them to heal every infirmity.

VERS. 2.-- *Peter and Andrew.* He joins the apostles in pairs and yokes, etc., *as far as* Christ, in whom he believed.

[0117D]VERS. 3.-- *Thomas.* The abyss: because by a sure faith he penetrated the depth of the divine power in the resurrection. Or, Thomas a twin, which in Greek is didymus, because of a doubting heart in believing.

VERS. 4.-- *And Judas Scariothis.* A great example of teaching for us, since he who knew all things did not hesitate to choose a betrayer for a disciple and to ordain him an apostle. For Christ has a witness conscious of his own cleanness, since he does not hesitate to choose his own betrayer.

VERS. 5.-- *Into the way.* After the resurrection he says: *Teach ye all nations.* But this beforehand: because the Jews must first be preached to, lest they have a cause for not receiving him, in that he sent the apostles to the Gentiles.

[0118A]VERS. 7.-- *The kingdom of heaven shall draw near.* [var: Vulg. Mt 10:7 *appropinquavit*, "hath drawn near"] Through faith the kingdom is near. For as one who sins is earth, so let the just man be heaven, in which God presides; whence it is said: *The kingdom of God is within you [n: (Luc. XVII)]*, etc. Behold what they ought to preach: The kingdom of heaven shall draw near.

VERS. 8.-- *Heal the sick.* The Church strengthens the sick by the standing of good work, raises the dead in sins, or without faith; cleanses the lepers sprinkled with errors, puts demons to flight by exorcisms. *Freely have you received.* Lest Judas, who had the purse, should wish to gather money out of the aforesaid power, the Lord suppresses his wickedness, saying: *Freely have you received,* etc. Here also he condemns the perfidy of the Simoniac heresy. Spiritual gifts are cheapened by a price.

[0118B]VERS. 9.-- *Gold nor silver.* Those who had these would seem to preach not for the sake of salvation, but of gain. *Nor money in your purses.* There are two kinds of necessary things: one whereby necessaries are bought, the other the necessaries themselves. By the money in the purses, that whereby they are bought: by the scrip, what is bought, what is stored there. Of this in the passion: *When I sent you without purse and scrip, did you want anything? But they said: No.* [var: Vulg. Lc 22:35 *At illi dixerunt : Nihil*, "Nothing"]

VERS. 10.-- *Nor shoes.* Plato too says that the two extremities of the body are not to be covered, and that softness of head and of feet ought not to be made habitual: But when these have firmness, the rest are stronger. *Nor a staff.* Matthew and Luke say *nor a staff;* Mark, *nothing but a staff:* by which [0118C] name, etc., *as far as* it may be shown by what way he ought to go upon the journey of preaching. *He is worthy.* Whence then necessaries? Take only so much as suffices for need, that thence being free from care you may better have leisure for eternal things.

VERS. 11.-- *Inquire who.* By the testimony of the neighbours the host is to be chosen, lest the preaching be injured by his ill fame. *Is worthy.* That he may know that he rather receives a favour than gives one. *There abide. [n: (AMBR.)]* He gives a general command of constancy, that they should keep the rights of the bond of hospitality: therefore a house is to be so chosen that no occasion be at hand for changing the lodging and for violating the bond.

VERS. 14.-- *Shake off the dust from your feet.* By the shaking off of the dust is understood the loss of the journey. *Shake off* the dust, for a testimony of the earthly labour [0118D] which they had undertaken for them in vain, etc., *as far as* they are said to have been washed by the Saviour himself.

VERS. 16.-- *Behold I send you.* Their punishment shall be kept for them in the time to come, etc., *as far as* he ought not to inflict evils, but to bear them. *As serpents.* The serpent's craft is, etc., *as far as* he puts off the old man.

VERS. 18.-- *For a testimony.* That thence the perverse may perish, etc., *as far as* the testimony of their innocence.

VERS. 19.-- *For it shall be given you in that hour what to speak.* Offer your will for Christ; but Christ will speak for himself.

VERS. 21.-- *And the brother shall deliver up,* etc. Less grief do those evils bring which are from strangers: greater [0119A] those which we suffer from those upon whose minds we had counted: because, along with the harm of the body, the evils of a charity lost torment us.

VERS. 22.-- *But he that,* etc. He teaches the virtue of long-suffering and of patience, etc., *as far as* we begin to possess this very thing which we are.

VERS. 23.-- *And when.* This belongs to that time of which it was said: *Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles,* namely that they ought not to fear persecutions, but to shun them: so that the occasion of tribulation may be a seed-plot of the Gospel.

VERS. 24.-- *The disciple is not,* etc. Do not disdain to bear what I bear, who am the Lord, doing what I will, and the master teaching what I know to be useful.

VERS. 25.-- *If the master of the house.* He shows his own calumnies, [0119B] that by his example they may bear injuries. Whence he said: *Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof. Beelzebub.* Beel is Bel himself, Zebub, a fly, etc., *as far as* the man of flies, or having flies.

VERS. 26.-- *Therefore fear them not.* Their savagery or their blasphemies, because the day will come when God shall judge the hidden things of men, where both their wickedness shall be uncovered, and your intention, now known to God alone, shall be known by all.

VERS. 27.-- *What I tell you.* That is, in what I wish you to be constant, etc., *as far as* the dwelling-place of the flesh being trodden underfoot, *preach ye.*

VERS. 29.-- *Upon.* He speaks according to the custom of Palestine, etc., *as far as* tell it in the whole world. *Are not two sparrows?* Luke: *Are not five sparrows sold for [0119C] two farthings [n: (Luc. XII)]*? Nor is there much difference, seeing that two go for an as, and five for a dipondius. For a dipondius is out of two asses. And what one is in numbers, that the as is in weight: and what two is, that is the dipondius. *And one of them.* How then does the Apostle say: *Doth God take care for oxen [n: (Luc. IX)]*? But care is one thing, knowledge another.

VERS. 30.-- *Numbered.* That is, by the knowledge of God, etc., *as far as* small and idle words should lie hidden from him.

VERS. 32.-- *Whosoever shall confess.* Or a man confesses Jesus with that faith which works by love: he denies who does not obey the precepts of God.

VERS. 33.-- *But he that.* He is denied by the Son before the Father, to whom there is not manifested, in the power of the divinity, [0119D] the Son and the Father. He is confessed by the Son before the Father, who through the Son has access to the Father.

VERS. 34.-- *Peace.* A good war was sent, that an evil peace might be broken.

VERS. 35.-- *For I came.* Here Luke says: *There shall be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three shall be divided.* How then, etc., *as far as* circumcision and the other carnal observances. *To set apart.* That is, to extinguish the private affections of the flesh, by which men so love one another that they serve God the less. Or that they be utterly turned away, not that father and mother are not to be honoured, but after God; this is the order of charity.

VERS. 37.-- *He that loveth father.* After God they [0120A] are to be loved, but if both cannot be kept, hatred toward one's own is piety toward God.

VERS. 38.-- *And he that taketh not,* etc. The cross is borne in two ways, etc., *as far as* the love of Christ may be shown. *And followeth me.* For one man mortifies the flesh for empty glory, or has a carnal compassion for his neighbour so as to favour his fault: he seems to bear the cross, but does not follow the Lord.

VERS. 39.-- *He that findeth,* etc. By the name of the soul the present life is designated.

VERS. 40.-- *He that receiveth,* etc. When he sends them to preach, etc., *as far as* that they ought to receive their wages.

VERS. 42.-- *And whosoever.* He who by the testimony of the shaken-off dust denounced the peril of those who do not receive them, [0120B] commends beyond what was hoped the desert of those who do receive them. Note that God looks rather to the devout affection than to the quantity of the thing bestowed. *To one of these least ones.* The least are those who have absolutely nothing in this world, and will be judges with Christ.



## CHAPTER XI.

VERS. 2.-- *Now John.* And while Christ was preaching, etc., *as far as* it does not appear who keeps the order of the thing done.

VERS. 3.-- *Art thou he.* He does not say *who hast come,* as if he should say: Since I am about to descend to the lower regions: I ought to announce thee to those below, who have announced thee to those above. Is it fitting for the Son of God to die, or art thou about to send another for these sacraments [0120C]?

VERS. 6.-- *He that shall not be scandalized.* He who shall not have doubted of the power of the divinity, he is not to be thought to have said this against John, whom he presently commends so greatly.

VERS. 7.-- *Concerning John.* The forerunner of Christ wished to make his disciples certain concerning Christ, because he perceived that they doubted. Concerning the forerunner, Christ taught the doubting crowds not to doubt, since they thought him soft and light.

VERS. 8.-- *Behold they who are clothed in soft garments,* etc. *Who put pillows under the elbow,* who soothe the life of sinners, and do not prick them.

A rigorous life and preaching ought to shun the palaces of the soft, which those frequent who flatter men clothed in soft garments.

[n: (CLEM. ALEX.)] Blessed John, despising even the hairs of sheep, which savour of delicacies, [chose] the hairs of camels, [0120D] etc., *as far as* he removed himself from all empty zeal, and from the vain appearance of good, and from a sordid and illiberal elegance.

VERS. 9.-- *More than a prophet. [n: (BEDA.)]* Because he is an angel not by nature but by office.

VERS. 11.-- *Greater than John.* In this he is not preferred to the patriarchs and to all men, but is shown equal to the other saints. *But he that.* That is, every saint who is now with God is greater than he who is still in the world. Or I, whom the opinion of many makes less, am set before him in the Church of the saints. Or the last angel of heaven is better than any man whatever. *In the kingdom.* The kingdom of heaven is taken in two ways: either the one above, in which we are not yet: [0121A] or the present Church, in which we still live, and already in a manner reign.

VERS. 12.-- *From the days of John.* The Lord had bidden the apostles go to the sheep which had perished of the house of Israel, that they might be brought back to the kingdom. But this preaching turned to the profit of publicans and sinners, who believed. For the rest, John is not believed by the people, Christ's works are given no authority, because the cross is for a scandal. Now prophecy ceases, now the law is fulfilled; Christ is preached to some, and received by others: his own reject him, his enemies accept him. And so the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, because the glory of Israel, owed to the fathers, announced by the prophets, offered by Christ, is seized and carried off by the faith of the Gentiles. Or, from the days of John, who preached his presence, by which the sinner comes to life again: [0121B] and not before, because the law brought in punishment and did not give life through penance. The heavenly fatherland suffers violence while the sinner enters into it, as into a place not his own, through penance. It is by a great violence to be born on earth and to lay hold of heaven, and to have through virtue what we cannot have through nature.

VERS. 13.-- *For all.* Not that after John there were not some, as Agabus, but because whatever they prophesied, they foretold of the Lord. *For all.* Because whatever they said, they spoke of one to come, but he pointed out the one who was coming.

VERS. 14.-- *And if you will receive it.* That you may be the less excusable, because you did not receive him. He is Elias in power, not in person, equal in severity of life, going before by rigour of mind Christ's first coming, [0121C] as that other the second.

VERS. 16.-- *But to whom,* etc. John being praised, he passes to rebuking those who were not moved by John's preaching: or who despise the preaching of Christ himself. John is such and so great as I have said, and so worthy that he ought to be believed: but to whom are you to be likened, who would not believe him? *He is like to children.* The children are teachers humble in spirit. Their synagogue, or Jerusalem itself, where the ordinances of God's precepts were laid up. Their equals, their fellow-tribesmen, whom they used to reproach, because they did not rise up to the praises of God with a devout heart, with the nimbleness of limbs which the dance marks. Nor by the lamentations of the prophets for the destructions already wrought or yet to be wrought were they turned to penance.

[0121D]VERS. 17.-- *We have piped to you.* As David: *Rejoice in God our helper, sing aloud to the God of Jacob [n: (Psal. LXXX)]*, and the like. *We have lamented.* As: *Be converted to me with your whole heart, in fasting and in weeping and in mourning [n: (Joel. II)]*, *and the like*

VERS. 18.-- *For John came.* As then, so now also you reject both ways of salvation. We lamented to John, we piped to Christ. This is the sum. This generation neither weeps with John weeping, nor rejoices with Christ rejoicing. Nor is it a wonder if they despise the twofold way of salvation, when they spurn both fasting and the fullness that is sought; if fasting pleases, why does John displease? if fullness, why the Son of man?

[0122A]VERS. 19.-- *And wisdom is justified,* etc. He shows that the sons of wisdom understand that righteousness is neither in abstaining nor in eating: but in an evenness of mind in bearing want, and a temperance in not corrupting oneself through abundance. The kingdom of God is not meat and drink: of which not the use but the concupiscence is blamed, in certain books it stands: Wisdom is justified by her works, because wisdom does not seek the testimony of the voice, but of works.

VERS. 20.-- *Then.* He who hitherto rebuked the Jews in general, now names the cities by name, which, having often heard his doctrine and seen so many signs, would not believe, to whom he does not wish evils, but foretells the things that are to come

[0122B]VERS. 21.-- *Woe to thee,* etc. Above, where it is read that Jesus went about the cities and all the towns, healing every disease: it is to be understood that among the others the Lord wrought miracles also in Corozain and Bethsaida. Corozain is interpreted *my mystery;* Bethsaida *the house of fruits* or *of hunters. If in Tyre,* etc. We now see this fulfilled, because Corozain and Bethsaida would not believe when the Lord was present. Tyre and Sidon afterwards believed when the Apostles preached: so devoted that all, with their wives and children, followed Paul as far as the ships when he departed from Tyre. Why then he preached to those who would not believe, and avoided those who would believe: he himself knows, whose ways are mercy and truth. Yet he purposed not to go beyond the borders of Judaea, lest he should give the Pharisees and the priests a just [0122C] occasion of persecution. And there were then those in Corozain who were to be called: nor yet were they to be punished more heavily for their contempt.

Tyre, *narrowness.* Sidon, *hunting.*

VERS. 23.-- *And thou, Capharnaum.* Not to Corozain and Bethsaida only shall there be woe, but to thee also, Capharnaum. *Shalt thou be exalted up to heaven?* Art not thou she who art made famous by the report of my lodging and of the signs wrought in thee, and hast most proudly withstood my preaching? Capharnaum is interpreted *a most beautiful village,* in which perfidious Jerusalem is condemned, to which it is said: *Sodom thy sister is justified by thee,* that is, by the comparison of thee with her, who was not corrected by the example of Lot, thou, to the words and miracles of the Son of God, hast always *proved* ungrateful.

[0122D]VERS. 25.-- *Jesus answering.* Answering of a tacit objection, as though it were asked what the reason was that the Jewish people, a worshipper of God, so obstinately rejected the Son of God coming in the flesh, whom the Gentile world so readily received? *Lord of heaven and earth.* Thou who makest the heavens, and leavest in earthliness whom thou wilt, or according to the letter. *To little ones.* To the wise and prudent he does not oppose the foolish and the dull, but little ones, that he may prove that he condemns swelling, not sharpness.

VERS. 26.-- *Yea, Father.* He speaks with the affection of one caressing, that the benefit begun in the apostles may be completed. Here we take an example of humility, that we may not rashly presume to discuss the counsels above concerning the calling of these and the rejection of those; for when he had brought forward both, [0123A] he did not at once render a reason, but said that it so pleased God, showing that what pleases the Just One cannot be unjust. In all things therefore which are ordered outwardly, there is the cause of an open reason, the justice of a hidden will. *Because so it hath seemed good before thee.* Lest anyone should again ask why he chooses the humble and rejects the wise.

VERS. 27.-- *All things are delivered to me,* etc. Understand mystically the Father delivering, the Son receiving. Otherwise, if thou takest it according to our frailty, when he who has received has begun to have, he who gave will begin not to have, by "all things" note the co-omnipotent, by "delivered", the Son, to whom by nature all things are his own by the right of one substance, not given through grace. But all things delivered are not heaven and earth and the rest which he made: but those who [0123B] through the Son have access to the Father, and who, rebels before, afterwards began to perceive the Lord.

*And no one knoweth the Son,* etc. To reveal himself. And no one knoweth the Father but the Son, and he to whom he willed to reveal the Father. For that which is subjoined refers to both. For by his Word the Father declares himself. And the Word declares itself, because it is the light of our mind.

*But the Son, and he to whom the Son will,* etc. A mutual knowledge, which is by equality of nature. But that little which is in us is of the condescension of him who reveals.

VERS. 29.-- *Take up my yoke,* etc. The yoke of Christ is the Gospel, which joins Jews and Gentiles in one faith. *Take it upon you.* That is, hold it in honour: not underneath, that you should despise it. You who labour, by the difficulty of the law, and are burdened with sins, namely, I will refresh you, [0123C] if you take up the yoke, that is, my precepts. And what is sweeter than his yoke? what lighter than his burden? to become approved, to abstain from evil, to will the good, to love all men, to follow after eternal things, not to be taken by things present, to be unwilling to do to another what thou art unwilling to suffer.

*Learn of me.* He teaching by word and by example, that you may be humble in mind, meek in manners. Humble, that they may despise no one; meek, that they may injure none. In heart, that the same be outwardly in work as in the heart, lest the serpent lie hidden in the appearance of a dove.

VERS. 30.-- *For my yoke.* How is the Gospel lighter than the law, when there works are condemned, here concupiscence also? But in the law many things are commanded which the Apostle says cannot be fulfilled: here the will is required, which is in our own choice, and which alone can suffice [0123D] and have a reward. Again, how is the yoke of Christ sweet, when it is said above: *Narrow is the way that leadeth to life.* But it is narrow, because it is begun only with a narrow beginning, but in the course of time is widened with the unspeakable sweetness of love.

*My burden. Because that which is momentary of our tribulation worketh an eternal weight of glory in the heavens [n: (I Cor. IV)]*. [var: Vulg. 2 Cor 4:17 *operatur in nobis*, "worketh in us"]



## CHAPTER XII.

VERS. 1.-- *At that time.* The preaching and the miracles of one year, done before John's question, having been related, he passes over to those things which were done in another year, namely, after John's death, when now in all things Christ is contradicted. *Being hungry,* etc. Because, as another [0124A] evangelist says, they had not even room to eat, for the crowds: on account of their exceeding importunity. The other Evangelists add: *that they rubbed them with their hands [n: (Luc. VI)]*. Whence also it is said to Peter: *Slaughter and eat [n: (Act. X)]* [var: Vulg. Act 10:13 *occide, et manduca*, "kill, and eat"].

VERS. 2.-- *It is not lawful.* According to the precept of the law. But because another scripture says: *I choose mercy rather than sacrifice [n: (Ose. VI)]* [var: Vulg. Os 6:6 *misericordiam volui, et non sacrificium*, "I have willed mercy, and not sacrifice"; the comparison is Migne's, and the gloss argues from it], it was better to free a man from the peril of famine than to offer sacrifice to God, since the victim that pleases is the salvation of men. Of the wasting of the crops they bring no charge, because by the law it is lawful to eat thereof.

VERS. 3.-- *But he said,* etc. In this deed we are taught nothing else, save that we should understand the sabbath not according to the letter, but spiritually. *Have ye not read.* If David and Abimelech are not reproved, each of whom [0124B] transgressed the commandment of the law under a probable necessity, and here the cause of hunger is like theirs, why do you not approve the same in the apostles?

VERS. 4.-- *The loaves of proposition.* Which signified that the priestly food would pass over into the use of the peoples. Or because we ought all to imitate priests. Or because we are all priests.

VERS. 5.-- *That on the sabbaths the priests.* Here he shows that the sabbath is violated without necessity by those very men who bring the charge. One example is given of the royal power, from David: another of the priestly, from those who by the ministry of the temple violate the sabbath, so that much less does the crime of the ears of corn plucked on the sabbath pertain to him who is the true king and priest and lord of the sabbath.

[0124C]VERS. 6.-- *But I say to you.* As if he should say: If the figurative temple could defend the priests that served it, why cannot the spiritual defend the disciples that believe in it?

VERS. 7.-- *But if.* And that he might show you that all things contain the figure of the time to come, he added: *But if you knew,* that is, that God has appointed to free the people by grace, and not by outward observances, you would not reprove mine, if they let the old things go.

VERS. 8.-- *For he is Lord.* If David when he was fed, and the priests who violate the sabbath by the ministry of the temple, are without crime, how much more the Son of man, who is the true king and priest and lord of the sabbath?

VERS. 10.-- *And behold a man.* This man is said [0124D] to have been a mason, because the hand to which the care of the spiritual building had been committed was withered until the time of Christ. *Behold a man having a hand,* etc. It signifies the human race dried up in the fruitfulness of good work, in requital for the hand stretched out to the apple, which hand the innocent hand stretched out upon the cross healed. Well was the hand withered in the Synagogue, because where the gift of knowledge is greater, there the transgressor lies under a greater fault.

*They asked.* Because he had excused the disciples concerning the violation of the sabbath by a probable example, they wish to accuse him himself, so that, if he should not heal, they may charge him with cruelty or with weakness: or if he should heal, with transgression.

*On the sabbaths,* etc. Chiefly on the sabbaths does Jesus teach and work, not only on account of the special sabbath, [0125A] but also on account of the more crowded gathering of the people, seeking the salvation of all.

VERS. 11.-- *What man shall there be.* By a fitting example he resolves the question, that he may show that they violate the sabbath in a work of covetousness who charge him with violating it in a work of charity. He reproves those who interpret the law ill, who say that on the sabbath one must keep holiday from good works. But one must keep holiday from evil ones only; whence it is said: *Ye shall not do any servile work therein [n: (Levit. XXIII)]*. That is, sin. So also in the eternal rest they shall keep holiday from evil things only, not from good.

VERS. 13.-- *Stretch forth.* Because nothing avails more for healing than largeness in almsgiving, whence it is said: *Let not thy hand be stretched out to receive, but closed to give [n: (Eccl. IV)]* [var: Vulg. Sir 4:36 joins the two members with *et*, not *sed*, so that the single negative governs both]. For in vain does he spread out [0125B] his hands to God when about to entreat for his sins, who does not stretch them out to the poor according to his power.

*As the other.* Man before the coming of Christ had his right hand feeble, because he was sluggish toward almsgiving: his left hand sound, because he was intent upon his own advantage: but at Christ's coming the right hand is healed like the left: because what he had gathered greedily, he now distributes in charity.

VERS. 15.-- *He departed thence.* Mark the example: *If they have persecuted you in one city, flee into another [n: (Matth. X)]* [var: Vulg. Mt 10:23 *Cum autem persequentur vos in civitate ista*, "But when they shall persecute you in this city"]. *They followed.* The learned, when they have seen his miracles, persecute; the unlearned, led by his repute, follow him in love, whence also they deserve to be healed.

VERS. 16.-- *And he charged.* Not out of fear, lest being betrayed he should be killed, but sparing the Jews, lest out of envy they should be slaughtered [0125C] in the face of his innocence and meekness. Here he instructs us mystically, that when we make much of anything, we should not seek praise abroad.

VERS. 18.-- *My soul.* By the soul every affection is shown.

VERS. 20.-- *The reed.* The Jews, yielding to every wind, who by disagreeing among themselves have been scattered, he will not straightway condemn, but will bear with them. *The bruised reed.* He who does not stretch out a hand to one that sins, nor bear his brother's burden, breaks the bruised reed. And he who despises the small spark of faith in the little ones, quenches the smoking flax: which Christ did not do, who came rather to seek that which had perished; for he kept patience, until the judgment that was being carried on in him should come through to victory, and, the prince of the world being cast out, [0125D] he should return to his kingdom, sitting at the right hand of the Father, until he put his enemies under his feet. *Smoking flax.* The Gentiles, whom, the ardour of the natural law being well-nigh quenched, the most bitter smoke of error, and hurtful of odour, wrapped about: whom he did not quench, but from a small spark he roused up into a great burning of the fire of God. *Until.* So long does his preaching, overcome by no snares, shine to the world, until he set judgment in the earth, and this be fulfilled: *Thy will be done, as in heaven and in earth.*

VERS. 22.-- *And he healed.* Three signs were wrought together, which are also wrought daily in the conversion of men, that, the demon being cast out, they may see the light of faith and praise God.

[0126A]VERS. 24.-- *In Beelzebub.* Beel, that is, Baal: of flies, on account of the filth of the sacrificial blood: he is the god of Accaron, by which name they call the prince of the demons.

VERS. 25.-- *Every kingdom.* He convicts them by a necessary dilemma. For either Christ casts out demons by the power of God, or in the prince of the demons. If by the power of God, they accuse him in vain. If in the prince of the demons, his kingdom is divided, and shall not stand: and therefore let them withdraw from his kingdom: which he hints that they have chosen for themselves, while they do not believe in him.

VERS. 26.-- *And every city.* The same reason holds of a city and of a house as of a kingdom. The city Jerusalem, ever glorious, after it blazed out against Christ and against the Apostles, division being made, fell in destruction.

[0126B]VERS. 27.-- *And if I in Beelzebub.* If the casting out of demons in your sons is ascribed to God and not to demons, why in me does the same work not have the same cause?

*They themselves,* etc. The contemptible things of the world, in which the holy simplicity of my power appears. Or rather thus: The sons, that is, the Apostles, who were well aware in themselves that they had learned nothing of evil art from him: therefore they themselves are the witnesses of my judgment, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

VERS. 28.-- *But if I.* That member: *If I cast out demons in Beelzebub,* has been carried through to many absurdities; now the other member of the dilemma is handled. *But if I in the spirit of God.* Here Luke says: *in the finger [n: (Luc. XI)]*. The Holy Spirit is called a finger, on account of the parcelling out of gifts. By the kingdom of God, either he means himself. [0126C] Whence elsewhere: *There hath stood among you one whom you know not [n: (Luc. XI, Joan. I)]* [var: Vulg. Jo 1:26 *medius autem vestrum stetit*, "there hath stood in the midst of you"]. Or the kingdom which John and Jesus himself preached. *Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven shall draw near [n: (Matth. XXI)]*. There is also a third kingdom, that of Holy Scripture, which is taken away from the Jews and given to a nation bringing forth the fruit thereof. Or the kingdom, that is, all the parts of the world, which he distributed to the Apostles and their successors to be converted.

VERS. 29.-- *Or how can.* The Lord therefore shows by a plain parable that he is not in concord with the demons in a deceitful working, as they falsely charged, but that by the power of his divinity he was freeing men from the demon; and therefore they commit a great crime who cried that what they had recognized to be of God was of the devil. For neither can they be in concord: [0126D] they whose works are diverse. Whence he adds: *He that is not with me,* etc.

*His house.* Or the house, that is, all the parts of the world, which he distributed to the Apostles and their successors to be converted.

VERS. 30.-- *He that is not with me,* etc. That is, he who does works unlike mine is contrary to me: he draws to vices, I to virtues.

VERS. 31.-- *Every sin and blasphemy.* What is contracted by human frailty is remissible, if the congregation be not forsaken. But if by diabolical obstinacy there is never a return from dispersion to the congregation, the sin is judged indissoluble.

*[n: (HIER.)] Every sin.* Not all sins are remitted to all [0127A], but to these, etc., *as far as* asserting that all shall obtain pardon after the universal judgment, though many ages have passed.

*But the Spirit.* He who manifestly understands the works of God, since he cannot deny their power, if goaded: out of envy he accuses, and says that it is Beelzebub, to him it shall not be forgiven. Not that remission would be denied even to him if he should repent: but because this blasphemer, his own evil merits requiring it, as he will never come to remission, so neither will he come to repentance. As John the evangelist says of certain men blinded by the desert of their blasphemy: *Therefore they could not believe [n: (Joan. X)]*. Which Isaias said again: *He hath blinded their eyes [n: (Isa. VI)]*. They who believe that the Holy Spirit is not, or is less than the Father, and say so: because they do this not out of diabolical envy, [0127B] but out of human ignorance, they are not held by an irremissible crime. But they who, in the likeness of the devil, assail the majesty of God against their own conscience, have no remission for ever, as Mark plainly declares: who, this testimony of the Lord being set down, subjoined: *Because they said, he hath an unclean spirit [n: (Matth. III)]*.

VERS. 32.-- *And whosoever. [n: (AMBR.)]* Even he who, being scandalized at the infirmity of my flesh, shall have suspected me a mere man or a glutton, it shall be remissible.

*But he that.* He who, not acknowledging the grace of the Holy Spirit by which repentance is inspired and return is made to the congregation, shall have remained with an impenitent heart: since this now is not human but diabolical, it will be irremissible [0127C]. *Neither in this world.* For certain faults are loosed in this world: but certain (the small ones, namely) even in the world to come. These indeed weigh heavy after death, but they are also forgiven, if a man by good acts in this life has deserved that they be forgiven there. *Neither in the world to come.* Because there are certain light ones, which, if in this life they are not yet remitted, weigh heavy after death, but they are also remitted, if they are worthy.

VERS. 33. *Either make.* For there is nothing between, but that the works of a good author are good only, and those of an evil author evil. He hems them in on this side and on that with a dilemma, and presses them with both horns. If the devil is evil, he does not do good things; if they are good, they are not the devil's.

*Either make,* etc. Mystically the good tree is Christ; the fruit, the preaching of the Gospel; the healings, redemption. [0127D] The evil tree is the devil and his own, that is, the Scribes and Pharisees: and the other evil fruits are envy, detraction, blasphemy, heresy and the like.



## CHAPTER XII. (cont.)

VERS. 34.-- *Offspring of vipers,* etc. He shows that they are an evil tree: and that they bring forth the fruits of blasphemy. *Out of the abundance.* A man is often deceived who weighs the heart by the mouth and by the deed. But God judges the deed and the words out of the heart, which he knows. To him therefore the mouth speaks out of the abundance of the heart, who knows out of what intention it comes forth.

VERS. 35.-- *A good man.* The treasure of the heart is the intention, out of which God judges works, so that sometimes the lesser works have a greater reward and the greater a lesser. In this place he either shows out of what sort of treasure the Jews bring forth blasphemy. Or it hangs together with the things above [0128A], that as a good man cannot bring forth evil things, nor an evil man good, so neither can Christ do evil works, nor the devil good ones.

VERS. 36.-- *An idle word.* If a man shall render an account for an idle word in the day of judgment, how much more you who say that the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub.

[n: (GREG.)] An idle word is that which lacks either the usefulness of rectitude or the ground of a just necessity, that namely, etc., *as far as* he shall here be held guilty not of an idle word but of a criminal one.

VERS. 37. *By thy words.* Death and life are in the hands of the tongue.

VERS. 38.-- *Then answered.* Since the Scribes and Pharisees could in no way disprove his words, they seek to tempt him in his works, seeking to see signs, [0128B] as though the things they had seen were not signs.

VERS. 39.-- *But the sign of Jonas.* He shows that the Jews are criminal after the likeness of the Ninivites, and, unless they repent, near to overthrow. But as to those men both the punishment is announced and the remedy is shown: so the Jews ought not to despair of pardon, if at least, after Christ has risen from the dead, they be admonished and do penance: because the death of Christ is the reconciliation of the world.

VERS. 40.-- *For as Jonas was.* Jonas, that is, one grieving, signifies him who bore our griefs. Or a dove: the fish that devoured him in the deep is the death which he suffered in the world. As he was cast out upon the dry land, so Christ rose again into glory.

*Three days.* After the manner of the ancients, who reckoned the day together with [0128C] the night preceding. Take the part of the day on which he was buried, together with the night gone before, for a night and a day, that is, for a whole day, by synecdoche. The night and the day of the sabbath entire. The Lord's night with the same day dawning, the part for the whole, and so thou hast three days and three nights. The first days are reckoned on account of man's coming fall from light into night. These on account of man's restoration, from darkness to light.

Mystically. *Three days,* three times, before the law, under the law, under grace. Three nights, the three dead whom the Lord raised up.

VERS. 41.-- *The men of Ninive.* And the sense is: Jonas in a few days and without signs preached to an unbelieving nation, and prevailed: I over a long time, and to the people [0128D] of God, and with very many signs, preach in vain. They are so much the more unworthy of pardon who are unfaithful though they have the law, by how much there is more faith in those who have not known the law. Ninive, *comely:* it signifies the Gentile world, which Christ loved when it was foul, that he might make it fair. In the Ninivites and the queen of the South the faith of the Church is signified, which is reconciled to God no less by repentance for folly committed than by diligence in learning wisdom. For there are two parts of the Church, that which knows not how to sin, and that which ceases from sinning, for repentance abolishes sin, wisdom guards against it.

VERS. 43.-- *But when,* etc. As if he should say: You are not like the Ninivites or the queen of the South: because when I preached repentance you did not repent, and when I [0129A] taught wisdom you did not learn. But you are like the man from whom the devil, being shut out, enters in again.

There is a difference between my works, who cleanse the things that are polluted, and Satan's, who more grievously defiles the things that have been cleansed.

*He walketh through places.* He explores the hearts of the faithful, cleansed from the softness of fluid thought, whether he can fix any steps there; and because he cannot, he returns to the damp places.

VERS. 44.-- *I will return into my house.* He sleeps under the shadow, in the covert of the reed, and in damp places. The dark shadow is the conscience: the reed, bright without and empty within, is the dissembler: the damp place is the wanton and soft mind.

VERS. 45.-- *Seven other spirits.* The seven vices, contrary to the seven spiritual virtues. *More wicked.* [0129B] Because he not only has vices, but also counterfeits good things. The more wicked, by so much the more crafty. Seven, because so many were the graces appointed with Christ.

Seven vices, seven demons contrary to the seven spirits, to the spirit of wisdom and of understanding, etc.

*So shall it be,* etc. What he said of one single case, this comes to pass in this whole nation. The unclean Spirit went out from the Jews when they received the law. He walked to the Gentiles, and when these afterwards believed the Lord, finding no place in them he said: I will return to the Jews, who stand empty of the protection of God and of the angels, cleansed by rebukes and chastisements, adorned with superfluous observances. Seven are added, because they that blaspheme Jesus are possessed by a far greater number of demons than they were possessed by in Egypt. Against the seven spirits [0129C] of the virtues is the number of the vices.

VERS. 46.-- *Behold his mother. [n: (RAB.)]* Mystically. The mother and the brethren are the people of the Jews, who, while Jesus teaches within, cannot enter in, because his words spiritually, etc., *as far as* The brethren of the Lord are his cousins, the sons of Mary his mother's sister: who is called the mother of James the less and of Joseph, and of Jude and of Simon.

VERS. 47.-- *And one said to him.* Insidiously, to try whether he would prefer the flesh to the spiritual work: and therefore he feigns not to know his mother and his kinsfolk by acquaintance, but says that they are near to him by the joining of the spirit.

VERS. 48.-- *Who is my mother?* He does not refuse the dutiful service of his mother, but prefers the ministries of the Father: he does not [0129D] despise the brethren, but prefers the spiritual work to kinship, that we too may prefer the spirit to the flesh. Whence: *He that loveth father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me [n: (Matth. X)]*. *Behold my mother,* etc. These are my mother, who beget me in the hearts of them that believe. These are the brethren, who do the works of my Father. Brethren and sister by believing, a mother by preaching.



## CHAPTER XIII.

VERS. 1.-- *On that day.* By this he indicates that this was done next in order, unless perhaps the day be put for the time, after the manner of Scripture. Mark keeps the same order. Luke passes to another matter, yet neither does he contradict this. [n: (RAB.)] Not only the deeds and the sayings of the Lord, but his [0130A] journeys also, etc., *as far as* to which the Jews did not enter in, fixed outside in the letter.

VERS. 2.-- *The crowd stood.* These are they who have lately come to hear, who are also set apart from the waves of the sea, and do not yet ascend with Christ, steeped in the heavenly mysteries which they desire.

VERS. 3.-- *He spoke many things.* Because the crowd is not of one mind but of diverse wills, he speaks to them in many parables, that according to their various pleasures they may receive diverse instructions. *He that soweth.* Christ himself, who sowed among men, by himself or by his own, the word of truth which he had seen with the Father. He who was speaking sacraments to the disciples went out to sow the word of God among the crowds.

VERS. 4.-- *By the way side.* The way is a mind trodden and dried up by the [0130B] busy passage of evil thoughts. There the seed perishes in two ways, because it is both trampled by the passing of thoughts, as Luke says, and snatched away by the birds. The demons are called birds, either because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature, or because they fly through the air. *And they came.* According to Luke it was trodden down by men, because it was taken away by the crooked persuasion of the wicked. *And they ate it up.* Because they stole it away from the minds of men.

VERS. 5.-- *Upon stony ground.* Stony places seek to sprout quickly, but the root is not fixed, because the earth is not deep, that is, because there is little of saving desire within. In this exposition of the Lord we learn that things are not always set down in the same signification. For the rock here stands for hardness, the earth for softness of mind, the sun for the heat [0130C] of persecution. Whereas elsewhere the sun is in a good sense: *The just shall shine as the sun [n: (Matth. XIII)]*, and the rock in a foundation, for the strength of faith, and the earth for earthly thoughts. *The depth of earth.* The depth of earth is the uprightness of a mind schooled in heavenly disciplines and proved in temptations.

VERS. 8.-- *Sixtyfold.* Because in the number six the adornment of the world was completed, by this good working is signified.

VERS. 9.-- *He that hath ears to hear.* As often as this admonition is interposed in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, it is intimated that what is said is mystical.

VERS. 10.-- *And the disciples coming,* etc. How do the disciples come to him, when the Lord was sitting in the boat? But perhaps it is to be understood that they had some while before gone up into the boat [0130D] with him: and standing there they ask.

VERS. 11.-- *To you it is given.* Mark that not only the words of the Lord, but his deeds also, are parables: that is, signs of mystical things, which many that are without did not understand.

VERS. 12.-- *For he that hath.* That is, to the apostles, who have faith, if they have anything less of the virtues, it is granted; from the Jews, who do not believe in the Son of God, even if they have anything of good by nature, it is taken away. For they can understand nothing wisely who have not the head of wisdom. *It shall be taken away from him.* He shall rejoice in no sweetness of true wisdom.

VERS. 13.-- *Therefore in parables.* It is said that they were blinded for this reason, and that the Lord's sentences were hidden from them by parables [0131A], that afterwards they might be more wholesomely converted. For because they did not understand the things obscurely spoken, therefore they did not believe in him, and so they crucified him, and so, after the resurrection, being terrified by miracles, they were pricked with the guilt of a greater crime. Whence, having received pardon, they burn with a fuller love. But John states this passage thus: *Therefore they could not believe, because Isaias said again: He hath blinded [sic: Excaevavit] their eyes, that they should not see [n: (Joan. XI)]*. Where he plainly says that the blinding was not brought about that, admonished by it and grieving that they did not understand, they might at some time be converted: for they could not do this unless they believed; but rather that they were blinded for this reason, that they should not believe, which they deserved by their other sins. *Seeing they see not.* As a covetous man has many riches and none, because they are useless to him.

[0131B]VERS. 14.-- *With hearing you shall hear.* These things were prophesied of the crowds, because they stand on the shore, and do not deserve to hear the discourse of the Lord.

VERS. 15.-- *Their eyes.* That is, they themselves were the cause to themselves that God should close their eyes.

*Lest at any time.* That is, therefore, because they would not open their eyes and ears, they did not deserve to be converted at any time: which nevertheless was done mercifully for them.

VERS. 16.-- *Blessed.* Truly blessed, because they deserved to see and hear even in the present that which none of the former men, of however great merit, deserved, however much he desired it.

VERS. 17.-- *And the just.* Luke calls the just kings, because they rule their own motions well

VERS. 18.-- *Hear you therefore.* He expounds the first parable [0131C], that they may attend to the same in the rest. He expounds it not according to the several words, but the sum of the meaning.

[n: (AUG. sup. Gen.)] Accordingly, what the evangelist related (was also done), namely that the Lord had spoken such things. But of his own, etc., *as far as* for that a narrator of things past wrote, this only a foreteller of things to come.

VERS. 20.-- *Upon stony ground.* They are sown upon the rock and among thorns who receive well: but either adversity by terrifying, or prosperity by flattering, holds them back from bringing to perfection. To riches is joined the anxiety of keeping them, which afflicts, and pleasure, which makes a man run to waste.

VERS. 22.-- *The deceitfulness of riches. [n: (CHRYSOST.)]* The things we have heard are choked by thorns, not indeed by the fault of the thorns themselves, but of him who them, etc., *as far as* [0131D] for there are in riches two vices opposed to one another, one which kindles anxiety and darkens with cares: the other which makes men softer with delights.

VERS. 23.-- *Some a hundredfold. [n: (RAB.)]* There are three differences in the good earth, as there were in the bad. For thirty is referred to marriage. Sixty to, etc., *as far as* the thirtyfold of the married, because this is the age of them that do battle, and to these the conflict is greater, lest they be overcome by lust.

VERS. 24.-- *Another parable.* As a rich householder refreshes those he has invited with diverse foods, that each one might take various nourishments according to the nature of his own stomach. Whence he also said another parable and not the other, that more may be understood to follow. This parable [0132A] is set forth, and, the crowds being dismissed, it is expounded at home to the disciples who ask. And here he teaches good will, and caution, and patience, and discretion, and long-suffering, and justice.

VERS. 25.-- *Men.* Those who are appointed over others in the Church for their protection and keeping: or when the apostles shall receive the sleep of death.

VERS. 28.-- *Wilt thou that we go.* When a spiritual man hears that this is from the devil, who avails nothing against the will of God, a will may arise in him to take such men out of the world, if he should have the power. But he consults the justice of God, whether he ought to do it, and whether God wills this to be the office of men. But the Truth answers: that a man does not know in this life what he will be who now errs, and what his error confers upon the good: and [0132B] that they are therefore not to be taken away, lest perhaps they be slain who perhaps are yet to be [good]: or lest it hurt the good, to whom they are profitable, etc. But that this is then done seasonably, when there is no longer a time for changing one's life and for profiting others: and then, he says, it is done not by men, but by angels.

VERS. 29.-- *And he said: No,* etc. Behold patience. For he did not blaze out into anger when the grievance was heard, nor did he wish to avenge himself at once; so let us also, when injured, bear it patiently.

*Lest perhaps.* Here place is given to repentance, and we are admonished not to cut off quickly: because he who errs today will perhaps tomorrow defend the truth. If therefore he were plucked up now, the wheat that was to be would be rooted out. Or it is necessary that the evil be mingled with the good, by whom they may be exercised. Or by comparison with whom they may strive toward what is better; and when these are taken away, [0132C] the height of charity withers, which is to be rooted out.

There the evil are to be borne patiently, where some are found by whom the good are helped.

[n: (AUG.)] A multitude is not to be excommunicated, nor the prince of the people.

VERS. 30.-- *Suffer.* This seems contrary to that word of the Apostle: *Put away the evil one from among you [n: (I Cor. V)]*. But as between the cockle and the wheat, so long as it is in the blade, there is little difference: so the Lord admonishes us not to judge concerning a doubtful thing, which the Lord in the day of judgment will condemn not by suspicion, but manifestly.

In suffering let us meditate justice: in judging let us not neglect justice.

*And in the time.* He who has borne long-sufferingly, by justice [0132D] repays what is deserved: for the virtues are distinct, but not contrary. *And bind ye.* In this life there is no binding, otherwise so many would not come to their senses out of error.

VERS. 31.-- *The kingdom is like,* etc. The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel, concerning which elsewhere: *The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you, and shall be given to a nation bringing forth the fruit thereof [n: (Matth. XXI)]*. Or the knowledge of the Scriptures. *To a grain of mustard seed.* It is compared to a grain of mustard seed for the fervour of faith, because it is said to drive out poisons, that is, all the doctrines of depravity. In the grain of mustard seed the humility of the Lord's incarnation may be understood. Which being received, a man put it in his garden, because Joseph, receiving the body of the crucified Saviour, buried it in a garden. It spread out branches in which the birds of the air shall rest, [0133A] because he scattered preachers throughout the world, in whose words and consolations the faithful might take breath from the weariness of this life.

VERS. 32.-- *But when it is grown up.* In the whole world, or in the mind of each: because no one is perfect on a sudden. It grew and became a tree, because he rose again and ascended into heaven. Or it shall have grown, that is, it shall have become known to the minds of men how great its power is. The rest appear as herbs, which grow quickly and fall: not living, but withered: that becomes not an herb, but a tree, where there are leaves with fruit, and in its diverse meanings spiritual men rest.

*Than herbs, and becometh a tree.* That is, than the doctrines of the philosophers, which grow quickly and fall, promising nothing that has life.

[0133B]VERS. 33.-- *In three measures of meal.* That spirit, soul and body, brought into one, may not disagree among themselves. Or the three powers of the soul are brought into one, that in reason we may possess prudence, in anger the hatred of vices, in desire the longing for virtues. Or, the woman, the Church, mixes the faith of men in three measures of meal, in the belief of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
